Line 253v.5: the edition's συννημένον is read as συνημμένον. Line 254r.2: διεζευγμένον is rendered "disjunctive" and τροπικόν "tropic". In 254v.1 the third mood is described as "denies by positing", like the fourth; this is the text as given. The fourth mood is again "from separation ... denies by positing" as transmitted. Line 255r.1: the edition prints a diagram of the division as stray words, and these are rendered as a bracketed list. Line 8: the edition marks a lacuna after ὅπερ, rendered [...]. 258v.6: συπέρασμα read as συμπέρασμα. 259r.2: the Republic premises as printed are lacunose; the second clause ("the wise man does not wish to have more than one like him, but") is supplied in sense from the parallel structure. 259r.4: πρστάσεων read as προτάσεων; "the Ethiopian" refers to the standard school example (black/white) run through the three figures. 259v.1: the etymological puns kalon/kalei and agathon/agan thei are kept by transliteration. 260v.1: ὃ read as δ′ (numeral four).

nodes.text: "In the same way up to the end of the three figures." After the syllogisms with assertoric premisses he presents the necessary [syllogisms], since the assertoric is closely akin to the necessary: for what holds, so long as it holds, is necessary; and the conversions behave alike for the assertoric and the necessary. For this reason the syllogisms too behave almost alike for the assertoric and the necessary. He says "almost" because of the fourth mood of the second figure and the fifth of the third. For in the assertoric these were not proved by conversion but by reductio ad impossibile and by ecthesis, and proof by reductio and by ecthesis, which in the other [moods] is superfluous, became necessary in these. In the necessary, however, they are not proved by reductio, since in the necessary and the contingent contradictories are taken by our opposing mode to mode, quantity to quantity, quality to quality; and so we fall into a mixture of contingent and necessary, of which we do not yet know what it concludes. They are proved by ecthesis alone, and proof by ecthesis, which in the assertoric is superfluous [except] in the moods mentioned, becomes necessary in the necessary. They are proved by ecthesis in this way. Let it be the fourth mood of the second figure: A [belongs] of necessity to every B, and of necessity not to every [C]. I say that B [belongs] of necessity not to every C. For since A [belongs] of necessity not to every C, let D be under C, to none of which A belongs.

Since, then, A [belongs] to every B of necessity and of necessity to no [D], therefore by the second mood of the second figure B [belongs] of necessity to no D; but D is some C; therefore B [belongs] of necessity not to every C; which was to be proved. Now let it be the fifth mood of the third figure, and let A [belong] of necessity not to every C, and B to every C of necessity. I say that A [belongs] of necessity not to every B. For since A [belongs] of necessity not to every C, A will of necessity belong to none of some [part] of what is under C, say D. Since, then, A [belongs] of necessity to no D, and B of necessity to every D, therefore by the second mood of the third figure A [belongs] of necessity not to every B.

That the assertoric, the necessary and the contingent are different. For the contingent neither holds nor is necessary, but is going to hold; and the assertoric is the contingent that has come about, and in this way differs from the contingent and from the necessary.

That the syllogisms of the three are also different, in that the premisses and conclusions are sometimes of the assertoric, sometimes of the necessary, sometimes of the contingent. "For the privative converts in the same way." But so does the affirmative; indeed, the affirmative more so, for it converts in the same way in all three, whereas the privative converts in the same way only in the assertoric and the necessary, but otherwise in the contingent. And for this reason he mentioned only the pressing [case].
In its own figure, even if not in its own mood.

That in the assertoric and the necessary, proof by reductio, which is superfluous in the second figure except for the fourth mood and in the third except for the fifth mood, has become necessary in the fourth of the second and the fifth of the third. That demonstration by ecthesis, which is superfluous in the assertoric in the fourth of the second and the fifth of the third, has become necessary in the necessary in the fourth of the second and the fifth of the third.
How did he prove, in the assertoric, the fourth mood of the second and the fifth of the third by reductio without opposing mode to mode, quantity to quantity, quality to quality,

if the assertoric too is a mode? For it signifies the contingent that has come about. For it is not the case that, if "holds not of every" is false, "holds of every" is true, since with [propositions] that have a mode the negations are formed according to the modes. Or else he then used "holds" in place of "is": for before the mixtures the assertoric is equivalent to "is", but in the mixtures it is a mode signifying the coming-about of the contingent. You will show the first from its being said that every premiss is either of holding or of holding of necessity or of possibly holding; for if holding too is a mode, where are the premisses without a mode? And the second from the mixtures being of modes: for "is" is always joined to every mode and never makes a mixture. The assertoric is not a mode, if every premiss is either of holding or of holding of necessity or of possibly holding; for where are those without a mode, if the assertoric too is a mode? Or: in the assertoric, when proving the fourth of the second and the fifth of the third by reductio, he took as contradictory of "holds of every" "holds not of every", not "does not hold of every"; for the negations of affirmations with a mode are formed according to the modes. That the assertoric is a mode, if he mixes it with the necessary and the contingent; for mixtures are of modes; for one does not speak of a mixture of what holds in the sense of "is" with the necessary and the contingent, since it is always present with them.
ON THE MIXTURES

"But it sometimes happens." After the syllogisms of the assertoric and the necessary Aristotle presents the syllogisms of the contingent. But first he mixes the assertoric with the necessary, for two reasons: either because the account of contingent syllogisms is intricate, or in order to complete the account of the assertoric and the necessary, the simple [cases] being known, and the compound too. By "assertoric" he now takes not, as in the three figures, what is in the sense of "is", but [what is] in the sense of the contingent that has come about. For if the assertoric in the three figures were a mode, the premisses without a mode will have been left out

(for he said there: "since every premiss is either of holding or of holding of necessity or of possibly holding"); and if the present assertoric were not a mode, there is no mixture, for every mode is joined with the bare "is". In the mixtures we do not ask [whether] a universal or a particular is concluded, nor whether an affirmative or a negative (for in these respects no change arises from what has been said, since then too the universal assertoric was taken as applying to the modes as well), but whether the conclusion is assertoric or necessary or contingent. When, then, a mixture of assertoric and necessary occurs in the first figure, Aristotle holds that the conclusion follows the major; if in the second, the one that converts; if in the third, the one that does not convert; for these become majors in the reduction to the first figure. But in the fourth mood of the second figure and the fifth of the third, which are not reduced to the first figure by conversion, the conclusion follows the worse. His associates, Theophrastus and Eudemus, and the Platonists, say that universally, here too, the conclusion follows the worse, just as in quantity and in quality. Of the later [commentators], Alexander and Iamblichus followed Aristotle, while Themistius, Syrianus and Proclus followed Theophrastus, Eudemus and the Platonists. That from a necessary major and an assertoric minor a necessary [conclusion] is drawn, Aristotle shows thus: if A [belongs] to every B of necessity, and B to every C assertorically, A [belongs] to every C of necessity, by the definition of "said of every". But A, they say, does not belong of necessity to every part of B, but only to its necessary parts; and C is not one of these, because the premiss BC is assertoric; for this reason C can be no part of B at all, when it is separated from it. And since A is inseparable from B, while B is separable from C, A too is separated from C, and therefore does not belong to it of necessity. Alexander,

pleading for Aristotle, proves the conclusion necessary also by reductio, in this way: if A does not [belong] to every C of necessity, it possibly [belongs] not to every; but B also [belongs] to every C assertorically; therefore by the fifth mood of the third figure, in which even according to Aristotle the conclusion follows the worse, A possibly [belongs] not to every B; but it also [belongs] to every of necessity; which is impossible, for these are contradictories. But, first, the proof is circular; for Aristotle will next prove the aforementioned proof of the third figure by means of the present mixture. Second, by the same arguments an assertoric, a contingent and an impossible [conclusion] are drawn as well: for if A [belongs] not to every C in whatever way you like, since B [belongs] to every C, A [belongs] not to every B, and I do not say simply; which is impossible, for it is laid down that A [belongs] to every B of necessity. So either all three are not concluded, or not the necessary either. The cause of the absurdity following when the conclusion is supposed necessary, and contingent, and assertoric, is not the mode of the conclusion, but that "to every" is concluded in truth (for from two universal affirmatives a universal affirmative is always concluded in the first [figure]), while "not to every" is laid down. Sosigenes, Alexander's teacher, said that what is concluded is necessary in the qualified sense: for so long as the middle belongs to the last, the major too necessarily belongs to the minor. But as far as this goes, even when the major is assertoric the conclusion is necessary; for again the major necessarily belongs to the last, so long as the major belongs to the middle; and every syllogism concludes what is necessary on a hypothesis, by the definition of syllogism; and in the second figure Aristotle shows a combination not concluding the necessary, because it concludes the necessary with qualification. Herminus said that the conclusion becomes necessary not always, but in certain matter; for if we take

animal, man, walking, a necessary [conclusion] is drawn; but if animal, man, moving, [is false the] contingent. For this reason Aristotle too said "but it sometimes happens". But Aristotle determined this by adding "but not when either one happens [to be necessary], but when the major is necessary". And he made the proof with letters, since he was making it universal. Theophrastus and his school argue their case thus: what is the arbitrary preference for the conclusion not following the worse in the case of modes as well? Or what is the arbitrary preference for the conclusion following the worse, according to Aristotle, only in the fourth of the second and the fifth of the third? And why does Aristotle prove the combinations concluding the necessary not through terms but only through the universal argument, while those concluding the assertoric both through the universal argument and through terms? Clearly it is because the assertoric is always concluded and he cannot find terms concluding the necessary, but in the universal arguments he deceives us; and every argument, if the facts are absent, appears something vain and empty. And if in the second figure the conclusion follows the one that becomes major in the reduction to the first figure, in the first mood of the third figure, from an assertoric and a necessary, both an assertoric and a necessary [conclusion] are drawn, since either can become the major in the first figure, even if in one case we need one conversion and in the other two. Or this is not absurd: for in the third figure everything concluded is particular, and a particular can be both assertoric and necessary; for example, white [belongs] to some animal assertorically because of man, and necessarily because of swan. The verdict, as the one who expounded this to me said, following Iamblichus' commentary, runs this way: from a necessary major and an assertoric minor in the first figure both a necessary [conclusion] is drawn, with the terms animal, man, walking, and an assertoric, with animal, man, moving; for the assertoric is intermediate between the necessary and the contingent, having from the

the necessary its being present, and from the contingent its being able to change to not being. And for this reason the assertoric has a range, and the assertoric premiss can lie closer to the necessary or closer to the contingent. And when it is close to the necessary, a necessary [conclusion] is drawn, just as a necessary [conclusion] is drawn from two necessary [premisses]; but when it is close to the contingent, an assertoric [conclusion] is drawn, as with the terms mentioned. † When Aristotle too says that from a necessary major and an assertoric minor a necessary [conclusion] is drawn, he takes the minor as close to the necessary; but when [he says that] from an assertoric major and a necessary minor an assertoric [conclusion is drawn], he takes the minor as close to the assertoric. For this is why, when the major is assertoric and the minor necessary, he calls the major "not necessary", excluding it from the necessary and seeing it as inclining towards the contingent; but when the major is necessary and the minor assertoric, he calls the minor "assertoric", and not "not necessary", as inclining towards the necessary. But even if we say, they claim, "rational [belongs] to every man of necessity, man to everything walking assertorically", although the minor is close to the necessary, an assertoric [conclusion] is drawn; and if "motion [belongs] to every walking necessarily, walking to every man assertorically", although the assertoric minor is close to the necessary, an assertoric [conclusion] is drawn.

That the mixture of assertoric and necessary is puzzling: for neither is an assertoric [conclusion] always drawn, as the Platonists and Theophrastus [hold], because of these terms: animal, man, walking: nec., assert., nec.; nor, when the major is necessary, is a necessary [conclusion drawn], as Aristotle [holds], because of these terms: animal [belongs] to every man necessarily, man to everything moving assertorically, and animal to everything moving assertorically but not necessarily; nor, as Iamblichus [holds], when the assertoric minor is close to the necessary, is a necessary [conclusion] drawn, because of these terms: rational, man, walking: nec., assert., assert. But neither

does a contradiction arise when we oppose mode to mode, quantity to quantity, quality to quality; for both "it is contingent that some man is an animal" and "it is necessary that no man is an animal" are false.

"But let B merely belong to C." See: when the major is necessary he does not call the minor "not necessary" but "assertoric", as being close to the necessary, although, when the minor is necessary, he calls the major "not necessary".

"But if AB is not necessary." A belongs to every B, B to every C of necessity; [he shows] that it is not concluded that A [belongs] to every C of necessity. For if A [belongs] to every C of necessity, since C also [belongs] to some B of necessity by conversion, A [belongs] to some B of necessity; but it also belongs to every [B]; which is impossible, for what belongs to every [thing] can also belong to none. Or also thus, in the third figure: if A [belongs] to every C of necessity, since B also [belongs] to every C of necessity, A [belongs] to some B of necessity; but it is laid down that it also belongs to every [B]; which is impossible.
"Further, it is also evident from the terms." Only now do you have terms, they say, Aristotle; for why not earlier too, when you concluded the necessary by false reasoning?

"But the animal does not move of necessity, nor does the man." In the examples too he calls the assertoric [premiss] that is close to the contingent "not necessary". For the proof is the same, by reductio ad impossibile and by terms.

"In the particular syllogisms." That in the particular syllogisms too, when the major is necessary, the conclusion also becomes necessary: for if A [belongs] to every B of necessity, it belongs of necessity to every part of it; and some C is a part of B; so A belongs necessarily to that part. But A does not belong necessarily to every part of B, but only to the necessary parts of B. The same holds for the privative too. But if the major is assertoric, the conclusion too is assertoric and not necessary; for that an assertoric [conclusion] is drawn can be shown by reductio ad impossibile, but that a necessary one is drawn cannot be shown by reductio ad impossibile. For [let] A [belong] to every B assertorically,

and B to some C necessarily; I say that A [belongs] to some C assertorically. For if "belongs to some" is false, "of necessity to none" is true, and not "possibly to none"; for the contingent is not opposed to the assertoric, since what now belongs may later not belong, and what now belongs is contingent, [being that] which, when it is not, but is posited to belong, nothing impossible results. And for this reason in reductions to the impossible the contingent should not be taken as the opposite of "belongs"; for they are not opposed in respect of necessary and impossible, but in respect of true and false. If, then, "A belongs to some C" is false, "A [belongs] of necessity to no C" is true; and C [belongs] of necessity to some B; so A [belongs] of necessity not to every B; which is impossible, for it belongs to every [B]; and the contradiction is "of necessity not to every", "belongs to every". But it cannot be shown by reductio ad impossibile that a necessary [conclusion] too is drawn. For example, I say that A [belongs] to some C of necessity; for if this is false, it possibly [belongs] to none; and C [belongs] to some B of necessity; so A possibly [belongs] not to every B; for a contingent [conclusion] is drawn here according to everyone, since the same premiss happens to be both the major of the first figure and the worse; but it also belongs to every [B]; and it is not impossible for the same thing both to belong to every [one of] the same and possibly not to every; for at the same time it is false, but not impossible, and later it is possible; so it is in no way impossible. But someone might say that, even if the impossible is not concluded this way, it is concluded another way: for if A [belongs] contingently to no C, since A [belongs] to every B assertorically, then in the second figure B [belongs] to no C contingently or assertorically; but it is laid down [to belong] necessarily to some; which is impossible. And that the conclusion is assertoric but not necessary, he shows as assertoric also from the facts.
Where does Plato say that in the mixture of necessary and contingent the conclusion follows the worse? In the first [book] of the Republic, in the conclusion

of the arguments against Polemarchus, with examples such as these: it is just to do harm to the bad and good to the good; to do harm to friends and good to enemies: nec., cont., cont. The just man does good to friends and harm to enemies; he does good to the bad if they happen to be friends, and good to the good: nec., cont., cont.

In the universal combinations of the first figure, when the minor premiss is necessary, if the conclusion is supposed necessary, a falsehood follows by reduction to the impossible, that is, to the false. But in the particular we cannot, by reduction to the impossible, conclude a falsehood when the conclusion is posited as necessary; for the combination becomes non-syllogistic, whatever premiss we add to the conclusion, since it is particular: for if we add the particular, it is from two particulars and non-syllogistic; if the universal, a second figure arises from two premisses of the same form, and so it is non-syllogistic. But the conclusion is shown to be assertoric by the terms: motion, animal, white.
MIXTURE OF ASSERTORIC AND NECESSARY IN THE SECOND FIGURE.

"In the second figure." That when a mixture occurs in the second figure, if the universal negative premiss [is necessary], as in the first three moods, the conclusion follows the universal negation; for this

becomes the major of the first figure in the reduction to the absurd; and it has been shown that the conclusion follows the major of the first figure. But if the universal negative premiss [is] not [necessary], as in the fourth mood, the conclusion follows the worse. And those [combinations] concluding the necessary he shows only by "said of every" and "said of none", but those [concluding] the assertoric both directly and by reductio ad impossibile and by terms.

"But if the affirmative premiss is necessary, the conclusion is not necessary." That in those from two universals, if the universal negation is assertoric, the conclusion too is assertoric, he proves in three ways. And he begins from the second mood of the second figure; for he passes over the first as simpler, because it needs one conversion. First proof: A [belongs] to every B of necessity; A to no C assertorically; I say that

B [belongs] to no C assertorically. For since C belongs to no A by conversion, and A to every B of necessity, the first figure has arisen with an assertoric major, and therefore an assertoric [conclusion] is drawn: so C belongs to no B; so that B too belongs to no C. Second proof: if B [belongs] to no C of necessity, C too [belongs] to no B of necessity; and B [belongs] to some A of necessity by conversion; so C [belongs] not to every A of necessity; but it also belongs to none by conversion; which is impossible. Or, as the text has it, C [belongs] not to every A of necessity; but it also belongs to every [A]; for if A belongs to no C, C too belongs to no A; and for this reason C can also belong to every A. Third proof of the same, by terms: animal [belongs] to every man of necessity; animal to nothing white assertorically; and man belongs to nothing white, unless, he says, one were to say "man [belongs] to nothing white of necessity, so long as", as the premiss says, "animal belongs to nothing white". But in this way every syllogism concludes the necessary, by the definition of syllogism. So in the conclusions one should not take the necessary according to the qualification.

"But when the affirmative is both universal and necessary." In two ways, he says, the assertoric is concluded particularly: both in the fourth mood, when the affirmative is indeed universal, and in the third mood, when the particular affirmative is necessary; for then the remaining universal negative turns out assertoric, and for this reason the conclusion [is] assertoric. So "and necessary" is added for the sake of the second [case], not for the first; for however the universal affirmative stands, as to assertoric or necessary, the assertoric is concluded.
MIXTURE OF ASSERTORIC AND NECESSARY IN THE THIRD FIGURE.

"But in the last figure." When a mixture of assertoric and necessary arises in the third figure, in the first mood, Aristotle says, the necessary is in every case concluded. Because in this figure the conclusion follows the

non-converting [premiss]; for this becomes the major in the reduction to the first figure; and the non-converted [premiss] can be necessary. But as far as this goes, says the philosopher Proclus in his school commentary on the first [book] of the Prior Analytics, the mood under discussion can also always conclude the assertoric, through the non-converted [premiss] being able to be assertoric. How then does the same mood conclude two conclusions, sometimes always the necessary, sometimes always the assertoric? Or rather, the argument would be insoluble if what is concluded were universal; but as it is, the particular can be both necessary and assertoric; for animal [belongs] to some white thing both of necessity, because of the swan, and assertorically, because of some man. In the second mood he holds that the conclusion follows the universal negative; for this is in every case the non-converting [premiss] in the reduction to the first figure; and if the universal negative is necessary, the conclusion too is necessary, but if assertoric, assertoric. And he shows each through the first figure, but the assertoric alone also by terms; for falsehood everywhere treads on emptiness, not being carried on things. And the terms are: good [belongs] to no horse assertorically; animal to every horse necessarily; and good not to every animal assertorically. And he takes exception to the terms because of the major premiss; for if the middle term happens to be not horse but venomous beast, the [premiss] saying "good [belongs] to no venomous [beast] assertorically" is false; for good is separated from the venomous not contingently but necessarily. And he corrects the terms by changing the major: for sleeping and being awake [belong] to no horse assertorically; animal to every horse necessarily; and sleeping not to every animal assertorically. In the third, fourth and sixth moods he holds that the conclusion follows the universal, whether it is affirmative, as in the third and fourth, or negative, as in the sixth;

for in these moods the universal is the non-converting [premiss]. In the fifth mood he holds that the conclusion follows the worse. So there are four qualifications of the conclusion with him for the present mixture and the present figure: one in the first mood, for the conclusion is always necessary; another in the second mood, for the conclusion follows the universal negation; another in the third, fourth and sixth moods, for the conclusion follows the universal premiss; another in the fifth, for [it follows] the worse. Or all these are one qualification, of this kind: when the proof is made by conversion, the conclusion follows the non-converted [premiss]; and it happens that the non-converted [premiss] in the first mood can always be necessary, in the second mood is in every case a universal negation, and in the third, fourth and sixth is in every case a universal premiss; but when the demonstration is not made by conversion, the conclusion follows the worse.

"But when the affirmative is posited as necessary, whether universal or particular, or the privative [as] particular, the conclusion is not necessary." Three combinations together, he says, conclude the assertoric, the remaining one of the sixth and the two of the fifth; for one of the fifth has the universal affirmative necessary, the remaining one of the sixth the particular affirmative necessary, and the remaining one of the fifth the particular privative necessary.

"So it is evident that." This is proper neither to all the figures nor to the third alone, but only to the first mood of the third figure; for this concludes the assertoric in one way only, namely only when both are assertoric; but the necessary in two ways, both when both are necessary and when one is necessary and the other assertoric, as has been shown. Conversely, the fourth of the second and the fifth of the third conclude the necessary in one way only, when both are necessary; but the assertoric in two ways, both when both are assertoric and when one is necessary and the other assertoric; for in these moods the conclusion follows the worse.

"But in both." That the mode of the conclusion is in every case anticipated in the premisses, as also the affirmative or negative, but not the universal or particular; for in the third figure particulars are concluded even from two universals. "In both", he says, [meaning] the simple and the mixed, and the simple in two ways, either from assertoric or from necessary [premisses].
ON THE CONTINGENT.
"About the contingent." After the assertoric syllogisms and the necessary ones and the mixture of the assertoric and the necessary he passes on

to the contingent too. And first he teaches those from two contingents in the first figure, then the mixture of contingent and assertoric in the first figure, and finally the mixture of contingent and necessary in the first figure; then those from two contingents in the second figure and the two mixtures in the same figure; then the same three in the third figure. And before all these he sets out in advance what the contingent is, the contingent conversions, and in how many senses [one speaks of] the contingent. The contingent, then, is that which, not being necessary, yet if posited to hold, nothing impossible results. For since the contingent is not yet present, but can be present and after being present be absent, because it is not yet present it is not assertoric; because it can be present it is not impossible; and because after being present it can be absent it is not necessary. For this reason he defines it by the negations of the assertoric, the necessary and the impossible: "that which not being necessary", since it is not necessary; "if posited to hold", since it is not assertoric; for if it were assertoric, we would not need to suppose it to hold; and because "nothing impossible results", it is not impossible. And it is well said "nothing impossible results", and not "nothing false"; for something false does follow, since even supposing the contingent to hold is false, even if not impossible. And that this is the contingent the reductions to the impossible show; for having said "if possible, let the opposite be", when the impossible follows we say that the opposite is not contingent, by the definition of the contingent, and in this way we make the proposition necessary. Aristotle establishes the definition of the contingent later from possibles following on possibles and impossibles on impossibles, but here as follows: if it is not contingent that it be, it is necessary that it not be and impossible that it be; so the opposites too: what is contingent to be, this is not necessary not to be and not impossible to be. And for this reason the contingent is defined by the negation

of the necessary and the impossible; for in general, of contradictions whose one members are true together, the other [members] too are true together. For let there be two contradictions, AB, CD, and let A and C be true together; I say that B and D too are true together. For if possible, let B be true of E, but D not; since then of everything [one must] either affirm or deny, and D does not belong to E, C belongs to E; so A too; but B too, by the hypothesis; which is impossible.
it is not contingent to be | it is necessary not to be | it is impossible to be
it is contingent to be | it is not necessary not to be | it is not impossible to be

2. The conversions of the contingent were not the simple ones (for he will hand these down after the first figure, where he needs them; for the other figures are reduced to the first figure by simple conversion), but the contingent ones, which change only the quality but keep the order of the terms. According to this contingent conversion, then, the universals convert with each other and the particulars with each other: by the definition of the contingent, what may belong to none may also belong to every, and conversely; and what may belong not to every may also belong to some, and conversely; and further the universals convert to the diagonal particulars; for what may belong to every may also belong not to every, through the intermediate "to none"; and what may belong to none may also belong to some, through the intermediate "to every". But universals no longer follow on particulars; for it is contingent that not every animal walks; yet it is not contingent that every animal walks, because of the reptiles. And this is what Aristotle [says]. But his associates, Theophrastus and Eudemus, and also the Platonists, do not hold that a contingent negation converts to a contingent affirmation, since the for-the-most-part contingent, which the discussion is about, does not remain. For syllogisms are put forward by the arts, which deal with the for-the-most-part contingent; for if it is contingent that no man is six-fingered
for the most part, it is contingent that every man and some man is six-fingered for the lesser part.

3. That 'contingent' is said of every kind of holding: necessary, actual, future; but of the necessary and the actual [it is said] for fear of the negation, for [otherwise these would be] what is not contingent; of the future, in the proper sense. And the properly contingent is twofold: either determinate, like the for-the-most-part; for this is determined, since it is more than it is not; or indeterminate, like the equally [possible] and the for-the-lesser-part. But in what way is the for-the-lesser-part indeterminate? For this too is determined, being more not than being. Rather, the for-the-lesser-part is indeterminate with respect to holding, just as the for-the-most-part is indeterminate with respect to not holding. Through what? Through at least two premisses. How? With the middle either only predicated, or only subject, or both. When? When the properties of each figure are preserved, as was also said in the case of the simple syllogism. Why then are these things added now too? Because some combinations that are non-syllogistic in the assertoric and the necessary become syllogistic in the contingent. I say that 'to be contingent' and 'the contingent' [are used] in seminal form: he has anticipated the meanings of the contingent, and later he unfolds them; for what the name signifies had to precede what it is, and not be put off entirely.
"For we call the necessary contingent homonymously." What does the conjunction "for" mean? Namely that he denied the necessary of the contingent, even though the necessary is [in a sense] contingent.
"Either they are the same or they follow one another." They are the same in meaning; they follow one another in expression, not being the same.
"For of everything [there is] either affirmation or negation." He hints at the lemma which says that if one member of two contradictory pairs converts, the remaining one will also convert.

"It turns out." The second heading: the contingent conversions; for he does not now give the simple conversions of contingent premisses, since he does not even need them in the first figure. How do all convert? Since the universals convert both with each other and with the particulars.

That it is not through conversion that "to every" is equivalent to "to some", or "to none" to "not to every"; for the quality remained. That the negations here are negations only in wording; for the mode remained intact.

"For example, 'it is contingent to hold'." That the indefinite affirmation converts with the indefinite negation, and "to every" with "to none" and "not to every", and "to none" with "to every" and "to some", but "to some" only with "not to every".

"And in the same way also in the other cases." For as "to every" converts with "to none" and "not to every", so also "to none" [converts] with "to every" and "to some". That he shows the universals converting with each other and the particulars with each other not through the definition of the contingent, for this makes the contingent [into] the assertoric; but by the fact that what is contingent to be is also contingent not to be: just as 'is' makes an affirmation in indefinite and unmodalized premisses, so also does 'contingent'. This clause has also been stated in [connection with] the three figures.

"Let us say again"; for he has already hinted at the meanings of the contingent. Or rather, earlier he stated the meanings of the contingent simply, but now of the properly [contingent]. And [he says] "again" because he mentioned the for-the-most-part and its opposite divisions also in [connection with] the three figures.

That the for-the-most-part is almost necessary, a necessary that lapses, and the for-the-lesser-part almost impossible, an impossible that lapses; for because of the for-the-lesser-part the for-the-most-part is not necessary, and because of the for-the-most-part the for-the-lesser-part is not impossible.

"Because a man does not always exist." Two causes of the for-the-most-part contingent not coming about: either the subject not existing or the predicate not existing; for a man naturally, for the most part, goes grey in old age, and reaches his prime and passes his prime; but he may also perish while still a youth, or even having reached old age not go grey, through some peculiarity of his stock.
"Or of necessity." How of necessity? Because upon the most proximate matter the form supervenes of necessity.
"And another, the indeterminate." Add: "in holding"; for the for-the-most-part is indeterminate in not holding.
That he applies "indeterminate" to the equally [possible] and the for-the-lesser-part, the examples show; for walking belongs to the equally [possible], and the earthquake to the for-the-lesser-part.
"What is possible both thus and not thus." This fits the for-the-lesser-part, but also the for-the-most-part.
"For it is by nature no more thus than the contrary." Because of the "more", this fits only the equally [possible].
That he calls the for-the-most-part "natural" because nature is occupied with it, and art which imitates nature.

"It converts, then." The contingent conversions, he says, proceed in both [kinds of] contingent; for in general the contingent can both be and not be. The difference is that in the for-the-most-part the affirmation is more true, but in the indeterminate either [both] equally or the negation more. However, he says, inquiries seek the for-the-most-part. So for this reason, Aristotle, you ought not to have adopted the contingent conversions. The natural can be and not be only because it is not of necessity; for it has a strong inclination towards being; while the equally [possible] is as it were a centre between holding and not holding, for it is equally distant from each. He passed over the for-the-lesser-part because the middle [term] is disorderly: for the middle is no more subject to the major than not subject, and no more predicated of the minor than not predicated; and arts that attain their end for the lesser part are lack of art rather than arts.

"It is not usually inquired into." Rightly, then, the Platonists do not admit the contingent conversions; for we seek them for the sake of syllogisms, and syllogisms are put forward by arts or sciences.

"These things, then." For in the second [book] of the Physics he will divide the contingent more clearly into the for-the-most-part, the equally [possible] and the for-the-lesser-part, and will distinguish the things occupied with them: that in some cases [it is] nature and art, in others choice, in others chance and spontaneity.
"And which." According to the mode of the conclusion.
"Since 'it is contingent'

that this holds of that." That "it is contingent to every" signifies two things: for A certainly holds of the things under B, by the definition of "said of every", but either of things that are contingently parts of B or that are actually [parts]. Let the first be taken now, since we are discussing [syllogisms] from both contingent [premisses]; but let the second await the mixture of contingent and assertoric. And so that there may also be a mixture of contingent and necessary, let "contingent to every" signify three things: that A holds of the things under B, being either necessarily its parts, or contingently, or actually; for, he says, the categorical [premiss] "A to every B" is equivalent to the one by prosleptic form "of whatever B [is said], A [is said]"; and B has different parts: actual, necessary, contingent. The same will also fit "holds of every" and "of necessity of every".
"Of whatever B [is said], A is contingent" must be understood instead of the assertoric.
"For thus." We know the conclusion, that premisses of the same mode are of like figure.
FIRST FIGURE FROM BOTH CONTINGENT [PREMISSES].

"When, then, A," and the rest of the first figure. [Having said in how many ways something is contingent, having defined the properly contingent, and having given the contingent conversions, namely that the universals [convert] with each other and with the diagonal particulars, but the particulars only with each other,] having given the meanings of the properly contingent, with each of which he wants the definition of the contingent also to convert, and having set out the contingent conversions and the present order, namely that after the contingent [syllogisms] in the first figure he does not give the contingent ones in the second figure but first the mixture of assertoric and contingent in the first figure, he discusses the syllogisms from both contingent [premisses]. Certain strange things happen with these: for no longer are all those in the first figure perfect, but some are perfect and some imperfect; and [a syllogism] comes about from two negations; and the syllogistic moods of the first figure are no longer four but eight; and there are no longer two properties of the first figure, that the major be universal and the minor

affirmative, but only one, that the major be universal. We shall begin the cause of these from the first, for the continuity of the account, making the end of the 'that' the beginning of the 'why'. Since, then, it has been shown that in the contingent, according to the contingent conversions, the particulars convert only with themselves, and no longer necessarily with the universals, for this reason the minor, even if it is a negation, changes into an affirmation and becomes syllogistic; but the major, if it is particular, does not change into a universal, and for this reason no syllogism comes about. And those that have an affirmative minor are perfect, as being shown through "said of every and said of none" alone; but those that have a negative minor are imperfect, as needing contingent conversion. And there are eight syllogisms of the first figure, since, the major being universal, the minor is either universal or particular, and in each case [there are] four ways by quality. So much, then, about the syllogistic moods.

All those that have a particular major are non-syllogistic: for since A is exceeded by B (for A holds of some B), let A be exceeded by B in the case of C; then A of necessity holds of no C; for example, white, moving, raven. But if A [holds] of no C of necessity, nothing contingent is concluded, not 'of every', not 'of none', not 'of some', not 'not of every'; and for this reason the combination is non-syllogistic: for if it were syllogistic, being from both contingent [premisses] it would conclude a contingent, just as from both assertoric [premisses it concludes] an assertoric and from both necessary

a necessary. And why do I say that such a combination concludes nothing contingent? For universally it concludes nothing, not the contingent, not the assertoric, not the necessary, since it concludes 'of necessity of every' thus: white, walking, swan; and 'of necessity of none': white, walking, raven; and insofar as it concludes 'of necessity of every', no negation is concluded, not contingent, not necessary, not assertoric; and insofar as [it concludes] 'of necessity of none', none of the same affirmations [is concluded]. Since, then, if it concluded [anything], it would conclude either an affirmation or a negation, and in each of these cases either contingently or assertorically or necessarily, and it has been shown to conclude none of these, it is therefore non-syllogistic. But one must inquire whether, so far as the terms set out are concerned, no syllogism at all comes about from both contingent [premisses] in the first figure. And if the contingent conversions are not to be accepted, as not preserving the 'for the most part' contingent, it is clear that Theophrastus and Eudemus and the Platonists will not disturb the notions concerning the first figure either; for it was because of the contingent conversions that there were imperfect [syllogisms] in the first figure, and syllogistic ones having a negative minor, and eight in number.
From the definition of 'said of every', not of the contingent, [that is,] from the definition of 'possible for every'.

"And are alike in position": so that again the major is universal and the minor particular. [Note] that of the eight moods he passed over the one having a universal negative major and a particular negative minor.
"For to this neither of every": for every contingent, universal, particular, affirmative, negative, is destroyed by 'of necessity of none'.
"Further, it is also evident from the terms": a second argument, more universal than the first, for those having a particular major being non-syllogistic.
It is evident that in the first figure, of the [combinations] from both contingent [premisses], those from both universal [premisses] are all syllogistic.
"But 'possible' must": one must not say that white is possible for every animal, since white holds of necessity of some

animal, for example a swan, and of necessity does not hold of some animal, for example a raven. If not only do the negations convert into the affirmations by contingent conversion but also the reverse, the non-syllogistic are no more syllogistic than the reverse. Or [rather] the negation must be changed into the affirmation, since they are all in effect affirmations, the mode remaining intact.
MIXTURE OF CONTINGENT AND ASSERTORIC IN THE FIRST FIGURE.

"If one is taken as holding and the other as possible". When a mixture of contingent and assertoric occurs in the first figure, these are Aristotle's doctrines: that those having a contingent major are perfect, and those having a contingent minor imperfect; for these, if the contingent minor is a negation, need contingent conversion, but if affirmative, they are shown through reduction to the impossible. Second doctrine: if the major is contingent, or assertoric affirmative, the contingent that was thought worthy of definition is concluded; but if the major happens to be assertoric negative, it is no longer the defined contingent that is concluded but the half-necessary. What this is we shall learn there. But since in reductions to the impossible, having supposed the opposite of what is being shown, he combines with it another false premiss, changing either the contingent into the assertoric or the reverse, and it is unclear on which the false conclusion followed, whether on the opposite of the proposition or on the substitution of contingent and assertoric, he therefore shows that the possible follows the possible and never the impossible, so that for this reason we may not ascribe the cause of the impossible to the substitution of the contingent and the assertoric (for this is possible, while what was concluded is impossible, and the impossible does not follow the possible), but to the opposite of the proposition. And this lemma contributes both to every reduction to the impossible

and to the establishment of the definition of the contingent. When A is, then, let B by all means be; and let A be possible; I say that B too is possible. For if [it is not] possible, let it be impossible; since, then, A is possible, let it be supposed to have come about; and since when A is, B is, then B too is; but it also is not, as being impossible in itself; which is impossible. Being unable to answer this proof, the Stoics raise a difficulty through examples thus: if Dion has died, ⟨this man has died⟩; and that Dion has died is possible, but that this man has died, when he is pointed out as living, is impossible. Similar to this also: if it is night, this is not day; and the first is possible, but the second impossible. Or [rather] the antecedent is wider than the consequent: for 'Dion has died' is true both when Dion is present and when he is absent, but 'this man has died' only when he is present. Say, then, 'if this man has died, Dion has died', and the possible follows the impossible, just as a necessary [conclusion] is also concluded from impossible premisses, and from Socrates' being a horse follows his also being an animal.

"If one [is taken] as holding and the other as possible": the syllogisms having a contingent major are perfect, those having an assertoric major imperfect; for they are shown either through conversion, when the minor is contingent negative, or by reductio ad impossibile, when the minor is contingent affirmative. And the privative syllogisms, that is, those having an assertoric negative major, conclude the half-necessary. But if the major is contingent or assertoric affirmative, the defined contingent is concluded.
One must take as possible: in coming-to-be, the properly contingent; in being true, the necessary; in holding, the assertoric.

"In however many other ways it is said": on account of the 'for the most part', the 'equally [possible]', and the 'for the lesser part'. Universally, then, the possible follows everything possible, contingent, assertoric, necessary.
"Further, 'when A is, B is'": since, in showing that the possible follows the possible, he supposed B to follow A,

now, he says, one must understand both premisses as A, and the conclusion as B; for from possibles [comes] a possible. But if the possible follows the possible, how is a necessary concluded from contingents? Or [rather], in that case it is not the middle term that is the cause of the conclusion but the nature of the extremes.
"For nothing is of necessity when one single thing is": understand in addition 'through a categorical syllogism', since when the sun is above the earth it is by all means day.
"When this has been shown": he teaches the use of the lemma stated in the theory.

"These things having been determined": after the perfect [syllogisms], that is, those having a contingent major, he teaches the imperfect, that is, those having a contingent minor, and first those shown by reductio ad impossibile, that is, those having a contingent affirmative minor. For let A hold of every B, and let B be possible for every C; I say that A is possible for every C. For if not, of necessity not of every; and since B is possible for every C, let it also hold of every [C]; since, then, A of necessity [holds] not of every C, and B holds of every C, the fifth mood of the third figure comes about from the mixture of the assertoric and the necessary, in which mood the conclusion follows the weaker [premiss]; therefore A does not hold of every B; but it is supposed also to hold of every [B]; which is impossible. Since, then, something at once false and impossible has been concluded, we shall surely not ascribe its cause to BC (for this is false and possible) but to AC. So if it is impossible that A of necessity [holds] not of every C, A is therefore possible for every C; which was to be shown. But it is not impossible, they say, that A should hold of every B and not hold of every [B]; for such is the assertoric; but only false, as BC also was. Or [rather] in the case of BC we change the time, but in the case of AB not; and it is impossible at the same time for the same thing to hold both of every and not of every of the same thing. He also shows this mood, both premisses

having been changed, BC from contingent into assertoric, and AB from assertoric into contingent; for it has now been shown that, when the major is contingent, the conclusion is contingent. But so far as this procedure goes, when the major is assertoric negative, too, a contingent is concluded. And what prevents using 'said of every' here too and making the syllogism perfect? For if [the objection is] that C has not yet become part of B, yet B too was not long since yet part of A.

"To produce the impossible": this is not strictly a reduction to the impossible; for the hypothesis of the opposite has not become part of the syllogism; and in this way one could call every direct proof [a proof] by reductio ad impossibile.
"One must take": one must not, he says, [take] the assertoric premiss as true by hypothesis

[as being] true, for instance 'man [holds] of every moving thing' assertorically (for this is true so long as only men are moving), since [then] there is no syllogism; for both 'of none of necessity' and 'of every of necessity' are concluded, as he proved through the terms. But we do not accept this interpretation; for Aristotle knows the difference between the assertoric and the necessary. Others interpret the same [words] thus: one must not define the truth of the assertoric [premiss] by the time of the contingent [premiss], and [say] that the assertoric is true so long as the contingent has not become assertoric, as here; for man holds of every moving thing so long as moving is [merely] possible for every horse; but if moving also holds of every horse, man no longer [holds] of every moving thing. One must not judge the truth of the assertoric by the time of the contingent, since [then] there is no syllogism; for both 'of none' and 'of every of necessity' are concluded. And for this reason Aristotle also said just before that it is absurd for the same thing to hold of every [instance] of the same thing before the contingent is realised and not of every [instance] after the contingent is realised. Nor do we accept this interpretation; for the second terms in the text do not agree with it; for in them, too, the truth of the assertoric is not judged by the time of the contingent. Perhaps, then, what is said is that in the assertoric premiss the predicate must be natural to hold of the whole subject, for instance 'walking [holds] of every man', so that we need a hypothesis only for its having been realised, and not also for its holding, as in the case of 'man of every moving thing' or 'animal of every moving thing'. These being taken in addition, [let] A [hold] of no B assertorically, B of every C contingently; I say that A [holds] of no C contingently. For if this is false, A of necessity [holds] of some C; and since B [holds] of every C contingently, let the premiss BC not remain contingent (for we do not yet know the mixture of the necessary and the contingent),

but let it become assertoric through the definition of the contingent; since, then, A of necessity [holds] of some C, and B holds of every C, therefore in the third figure, in which the conclusion follows the unconverted [premiss], the proof being made by conversion, A holds of some B; but [it holds] also of none; which is impossible; therefore A does not of necessity [hold] of some C; therefore it is possible for it [to hold] of none; which was proposed to be shown. However, he says, it is not the qualified contingent that is concluded but the half-contingent and the half-necessary, which he calls 'of none of necessity', because it is true both of 'of necessity of none' and of 'possibly of none'. For 'possibly of none', he says, is true together with 'possibly of every'; and to 'possibly of none' is opposed 'of necessity of some', while to 'possibly of every' [is opposed] 'of necessity not of every'; so that both at once conflict contradictorily with 'possibly of none': 'of necessity of some' because of 'possibly of none' itself, and 'of necessity not of every' because of 'possibly of every'; for indeed it is not true [that everything is] either 'possibly of none' or 'of necessity of some', since both are false of 'every man is winged'. So whoever is going to establish 'possibly of none' must do away with both opposites, 'of necessity of some' and 'of necessity not of every'. But here nothing absurd follows from 'of necessity not of every'; for [the result] is also the fifth mood of the third figure, in which the conclusion follows the weaker [premiss]; and for this reason A holds not of every B; but it was also holding of none; and [there is] nothing absurd, but indeed [it is] necessary. Since, then, only 'of necessity of some' has been done away with, and not also 'of necessity not of every', both of which are opposed to 'possibly of none', the contingent and the necessary have been done away with by half; and for this reason what is concluded is half contingent and [half] necessary, which he calls 'of none of necessity', since 'of some' has been done away with and since 'of none of necessity' is said both of 'of necessity of none' and of 'possibly of none'. Therefore

the contradictions in this treatise are not rightly taken when we oppose mode to mode, quantity to quantity, quality to quality; for 'possibly of none' is contradicted not by 'of necessity of some' alone but together with 'of necessity not of every'; and the two at once as one, 'possibly of every' and 'possibly of none', contradict the two at once as one, 'of necessity of some' and 'of necessity not of every'. For not everything is either 'possibly of none' or 'of necessity of some'; for in the case of 'every man is winged', both 'possibly of none' is false (for man is of necessity not winged) and 'of necessity of some'. Likewise not everything is either 'possibly of every' or 'of necessity not of every'; for both are false in the case of 'every man is an animal'. possibly of none possibly of every possibly of some possibly not of every contradiction contradiction of necessity of none of necessity of every of necessity of some of necessity not of every
"For this is the contradiction": for 'of none of necessity' contradicts 'of necessity of some'; for he does not establish by reductio ad impossibile the opposite of what is done away with.

"For let A be": the terms have not been well taken; for raven holds of nothing thinking necessarily, not assertorically; and knowledge is necessarily not moving, unless perhaps we take knowledge as the knower. And it is chiefly because of the first charge that he adds 'but the terms must be taken better'; for instance white [holds] of every swan of necessity, with moving as middle, and white of no raven of necessity, with the same as middle.
"Which is true": yet it is false, even if possible, to suppose the contingent as holding. 'Which is true', then, [means] in potentiality, even if not in actuality.
"Common terms": here too the terms must be taken better; for animal necessarily does not hold of snow and pitch. Moving must be taken as the middle term in both combinations.
That in [syllogisms] from two universals, when the minor is contingent, a syllogism always comes about.

"Except that sometimes from themselves": yet all that have the minor contingent are imperfect. 'From themselves', then, not as perfect but as needing the change in quality: if the minor is affirmative, by reductio ad impossibile; if negative, first by conversion (for the contingent is naturally such as both to hold and not to hold), then by reductio ad impossibile, since the syllogism we use is also affirmative.

"If one is universal and the other particular": those that have the major universal contingent and the minor particular assertoric affirmative are perfect; for they are shown through 'said of every and said of none'; and they conclude the contingent in the strict sense.

"If universal": those that have the major universal assertoric and the minor particular contingent are imperfect; for if the minor is affirmative, they are shown by reductio ad impossibile; if negative, they first need conversion, then [proof] by reductio ad impossibile; for 'others by conversion' is equivalent to 'others both by conversion [and by reductio]', as also in the case of the universal. And if the major is assertoric negative, the half-necessary and [half-]contingent is concluded here too, but [if it is] assertoric affirmative, the contingent in the strict sense.

"There will be a syllogism through conversion": if the minor is contingent particular negative, there will be a syllogism; for it can change into an affirmation; but if it is assertoric particular negative, there is no syllogism; for 'not of every' is true also in the case of 'of none'; and when the minor is assertoric universal negative it has been shown that no syllogism comes about.

"Terms for": here too the terms must be taken better; for white [holds] of some animal of necessity and of necessity not of every animal; and animal of necessity [holds] of no motion or pitch. The sound terms, then, for 'of every of necessity' are moving, white, walking; for 'of none of necessity', moving, white, standing.
"Whether taking possibility
or holding or alternately": only the third is proper to the present discussion, but as lovers of the universal we have included the first two as well.

"It is evident that when the universal is placed in relation to the major extreme there is always a syllogism": what then, even if the minor [premise], being assertoric, is negative? Or [rather]: when the minor is affirmative and the major is affirmative 〈or negative〉, and the major universal, there is always a syllogism, however the assertoric and the contingent stand in order.
MIXTURE OF CONTINGENT AND NECESSARY.

"If one [premise is taken as] holding or not holding of necessity, and the other as being possible": Of the eight combinations that arise from both [premises] universal, two are non-syllogistic, those having the minor necessary negative, for the fault is incurable; the remaining six are syllogistic. Of these, two are perfect, those having the minor necessary affirmative; four are imperfect, those having the minor contingent. Of these, two are proved by reductio ad impossibile, those having the minor contingent affirmative; and two need conversion before the proof by the impossible, those having the minor contingent negative. And of the syllogistic ones, two conclude the half-contingent and [half-]necessary, that is, the assertoric: those having the necessary negative, and that as major in every case; and four [conclude] the contingent in the strict sense, those having the necessary affirmative; for [they are] either from premises of like form or from premises of unlike form, and each of these in two ways according to the order of the modes. And in short, as much as the assertoric produced in the mixture of contingent and assertoric, so much does the necessary produce in the mixture of contingent and necessary. And the moods are the same in the case of necessary and contingent, both for those from both [premises] universal and for those with one universal, perfect and imperfect alike, and concluding the contingent in the strict sense or the half-[contingent]; the only difference is that now the half-contingent is the assertoric. Those having the
minor contingent are imperfect: what is peculiar to the minor makes no difference when it is contingent, but if it is assertoric, it does make a difference.

Two are non-syllogistic, 〈those〉 having the minor necessary negative, and six syllogistic, those not having the minor necessary negative. Of these, four are imperfect, those having the minor contingent: the first, third, fifth, sixth; by reductio ad impossibile the first and third, by conversion the fifth and sixth. Two are perfect, those having the minor necessary affirmative: the second and fourth. Two conclude the half-necessary, those having the necessary negative: the third and sixth; four the contingent in the strict sense, those having the necessary affirmative: the first, second, fourth, fifth.

First mood. A [holds] of every B of necessity, B possibly of every C: the syllogism is imperfect and by reductio ad impossibile, and concludes the contingent in the strict sense. I say, then, that A possibly [holds] of every C; for if not this, then of necessity of some, or of necessity not of every; but both are impossible. For let it first be that A [holds] of C of necessity not of every; and since B possibly [holds] of every C, B therefore holds of every C; since, then, A [holds] of C of necessity not of every, and B holds of every C, there arises the fifth mood of the third figure, in which the conclusion follows the weaker [premise]; therefore A holds not of every B; but also [it holds] of every [B] of necessity; which is impossible. But now let it be supposed that A [holds] of C of necessity of some; since A [holds] of some C of necessity, and B holds of every C, in the third figure the conclusion follows the [premise] that is not converted, and
A holds of some B; but also of necessity of every; which is impossible.

Second mood. A possibly [holds] of every B, B of every C of necessity: perfect, concluding the contingent in the strict sense through 'said of every'. We did not use 'said of every' earlier too, since C had not yet become a part of B as [it has] now.

Third mood. A [holds] of no B of necessity, B possibly of every C: imperfect, concluding the assertoric by reductio ad impossibile. For if it is false that A holds of no C, A holds of some C; but B also holds of every C; in the third figure, from both assertoric, A holds of some B; but also of necessity of none; which is impossible. But the contradiction was not taken soundly; for the mode remained, and as far as this argument goes, 'of necessity of none' is also concluded; for if A [does] not [hold] of C of necessity of none, A [holds] of C of necessity of some; but A [holds] also of B of necessity of none; therefore B [holds] of C of necessity not of every; but also possibly of every; which is absurd. So the absurdity followed not because of the mode, but because 'of none' was supposed [to be] 'of some'. Here too, then, the conclusion follows the weaker [premise], and a contingent is concluded, not an assertoric.

Fourth mood. A possibly [holds] of no B, B of every C of necessity: perfect, concluding the contingent in the strict sense through 'said of every'. For it is not possible to refute 'possibly of none'; for which [premise] would one add? If AB, the two are negative; if BC, we do not have a mixture of contingent and necessary in the third figure.

Fifth mood. A [holds] of every B of necessity, B possibly of no C: the syllogism is imperfect, concluding the contingent in the strict sense by contingent conversion and by reductio ad impossibile, like the first mood.
Sixth mood. A [holds] of no B of necessity, B possibly of no
C: imperfect, concluding the assertoric by contingent conversion and by reductio ad impossibile, like the third mood.

"In the same way also with particular syllogisms": with these he sets down first the [combinations] of unlike form, as being varied; for of those of unlike form some conclude a contingent, others an assertoric; but all those of like form conclude a contingent. And for this reason he places the fourth mood before the third.

A [holds] of B of necessity of none, B possibly of some C: I say that A holds not of every C. * * * and B [holds] of A of necessity of none, because of the conversion of the universal privative; therefore B [holds] of C of necessity of none; for a mixture of necessary and assertoric has arisen in the first figure, and the major is necessary, so that the conclusion follows the major; but it is supposed that B possibly [holds] of some C; which is impossible. But, say the Platonists, it must thus be conceded that in the first figure the conclusion follows the major in the mixture of necessary and assertoric. And as far as this argument goes, the proposed combination also concludes 'of necessity not of every'; for if this is false, A [holds] of C of necessity of every; and B [holds] of A of necessity of none; therefore in the first figure, from two necessary [premises], B [holds] of C of necessity of none; but also possibly of some. Since, then, in truth 'not of every' is concluded and 'of every' was supposed, the impossibility [arises] not because of the assertoric or the necessary, as in the case of those from both universal. But the Platonists, wishing the conclusion always to follow the weaker [premise], object to these mixtures alone, those that conclude an assertoric.
2. A possibly [holds] of no B, B of some C of necessity: the syllogism is perfect and of the contingent; for the proof is through 'said of none'.

3. A [holds] of every B of necessity, B possibly of some C: the syllogism is of the contingent; for if it is false that A possibly [holds] of some C, A [holds] of no C of necessity; but A also [holds] of every B of necessity; from two necessary [premises] in the second figure, B [holds] of no C of necessity; but also possibly of some; which is impossible. It is possible here too to say that half of the contingent is concluded; for to 'possibly of some' two things are opposed: 'of necessity of none', which has been refuted, and 'of necessity of every', from which nothing absurd follows.
"If the universal is placed in relation to the minor extreme": all those having the major particular are non-syllogistic. These are fourfold, as is set out below,
and the text presents them according to the numbers set beneath.
"Either affirmative or privative or contingent": that is, also contingent; for the contingent is not opposed to affirmation and negation.

"For animal [holds] of some white": that is, the same terms produce both 'of necessity of some' and 'of necessity not of every' and 'possibly of some' and 'possibly not of every'; for animal [holds] of some white of necessity because of the swan, and of necessity not of every because of the raven, and possibly of some and possibly not of every because of the men among the Ethiopians or Gauls. And the four hold also in the case of white and inanimate, because of white lead, ebony, and the things to which it can possibly belong.

"It is evident, then, from what has been said" that those having the major particular are non-syllogistic, both in those from two alike [premises] and in the mixed ones. And under these are ranked also those having the minor necessary negative.

Except that, when the contingent and the assertoric were mixed, those having the major assertoric negative concluded the half-contingent and half-necessary (for 'of necessity of none' is carried over both onto 'of necessity of none' and onto 'possibly of none';

and for this reason either the necessary or the contingent was concluded), whereas when there is a mixture of contingent and necessary, when the major is a necessary universal negative, the assertoric is concluded, which is something other than the necessary and the contingent.

"It is clear that all the syllogisms are also incomplete." But not all are incomplete; for certainly not those having the minor necessary, but only those having the minor contingent. Or what is said is this: all those having the minor contingent are incomplete, since even if it is affirmative, they are incomplete.

"And that they are completed through the figures mentioned before." They are completed through the first figure alone; but he spoke in the plural, since the reduction to the impossible produced a first figure either unmixed, from two necessary [premises], or mixed, from necessary and assertoric. And the text calls the half-contingent both assertoric and contingent.
SECOND FIGURE FROM TWO CONTINGENT [PREMISES].

"In the second figure." Earlier Aristotle, in the three figures, divided the moods according to the figures, for instance [the premises] from two assertoric into first figure and second and third, and those from two necessary, and the mixtures of these. But now, in the mixtures, he divides the figures according to the moods, for instance the first figure into those from two contingent and the mixtures of contingent and assertoric, and of contingent and necessary. For if he had used the earlier order, he would have placed those from two contingent in the second figure before the mixtures in the first figure of assertoric

and contingent, assertoric and necessary, contingent and necessary; which is absurd; for those from two contingent in the second figure are non-syllogistic, while the three mixtures in the first figure are divided into the syllogistic and the non-syllogistic. But since those in the second figure are proved by being reduced to the first figure either through conversion or by reductio ad impossibile, he discusses the simple conversion of contingent premises; and since, when the second figure is proved through conversion, it is always the universal negative that is converted, he discusses only the conversion of the contingent universal negative, and shows that the contingent universal negative does not convert into itself. And he told us this too in the three figures, that the affirmatives of the contingent, like the assertoric and the necessary, convert into the particular affirmative, but the contingent universal negative not alike; for in the assertoric and necessary it converts into itself, but in the contingent it does not convert into itself: "this will be clear", he said, "when we speak about the contingent". That, then, the universal contingent negative does not convert into itself, he now shows, and he advances the proof in three ways. And first thus: if A possibly [holds] of no B, it is not necessary that B also possibly [holds] of no A; for if so, the universal affirmative also converts into itself, as I shall show; but this is impossible; for white can possibly hold of every animal, but it is no longer [true] that animal can possibly hold of every white; for of some white, white lead, it of necessity does not hold. And the conditional is to be shown thus: if A can possibly hold of no B, B too can possibly hold of no A; since indeed what possibly [holds] of none also possibly [holds] of every, according to contingent conversion, A also possibly [holds] of every B, and B possibly of every A. But the Platonists would say to this: it is not the case that if A possibly [holds] of no B, it thereby possibly [holds] of every, in the case of the contingent for the most part, but if at all, only in the case of the equally [possible]. Aristotle

would say: but the contingent has remained in its species. The second argument [is] through the same terms by which he refuted the universal negative as not converting into itself: for white can possibly hold of no man; yet man cannot possibly hold of no white; for of the swan and white lead it necessarily does not hold. But the Platonists would say regarding the terms: what sort of white do you take? If white simply, then neither is the original negative, 'white can possibly hold of no man', contingent; for the white in a swan necessarily does not hold of man; but if the white in man, then it is possible both for white to hold of no man and for man [to hold] of no white. But the Peripatetics would say that the question is not fairly put, because the determinations are not attached to the predicate but to the subject, and that, so far as this goes, the necessary universal affirmative would also convert into itself. And the Platonists would say that the terms too have not been soundly taken; for they are equally [possible] and not for the most part; but if we take [terms] for the most part, the contingent universal negative converts into itself; for it is possible that no man is six-fingered, and it is possible that nothing six-fingered is a man. The third argument of the text, that the contingent universal negative does not convert into itself: for if someone were to say thus, 'if A possibly [holds] of no B, B also possibly [holds] of no A; for if not, of necessity of some; so that A too converts to B; but it was also possibly of none; which is impossible', the one who says this reasons fallaciously; for to 'possibly of none' is opposed not only 'of necessity of some' but also 'of necessity not of every'; when this is assumed, nothing impossible results; for the particular negative does not convert. But the Platonists would say: and how did Aristotle himself, in the three figures, show that both contingent affirmatives convert into the particular affirmative? For he said: if A possibly [holds] of every or of some B,

B too possibly [holds] of some A; for if this is false, of necessity of none; for we too shall say to you that to 'possibly of some' is opposed not only 'of necessity of none' but also 'of necessity of every'; when this is assumed, nothing impossible follows, since A possibly [holds] of every B, even if, as much as you like, something impossible follows if A possibly [holds] of some B. And the Platonists would say that they have not used the proof criticised by Aristotle but another, of this sort: if A is contingently separated from B, B too is contingently separated from A, and for this reason the universal negative converts into itself also in the case of the contingent.

Why in the second figure from two contingent [premises] does no syllogism come about? For not only can those of unlike form become of like form, but also those of like form [can become] of unlike form. Or because for being non-syllogistic it suffices sometimes not to conclude, but for being syllogistic it does not suffice sometimes to conclude, but only always.

Why in the second figure, in the mixture of contingent and assertoric, are those having the assertoric negative syllogistic, but those having the assertoric affirmative non-syllogistic? For if [it is] because it is possible to make them of like form, even if they are of unlike form, it is also possible to make them of unlike form. Or because the negative is not strictly a negative but an unclear affirmative, and becomes a clearer affirmative when taken into an affirmative, whereas the affirmative is in no way the contradictory negative, and for this reason is not changed into it.

"One must take [them] in these cases too." That is, as in the first figure, so also in the second, the same combinations either conclude the contingent in the strict sense or do not, but [conclude] either the half-[contingent] or the assertoric.

"Both the contrary and the opposed." Contraries are 'every' and 'none', and those under them, 'some' and 'not every'; opposed are the contradictories, the diagonal ones; for these too convert; for if 'every',

then also 'some' and 'not every'; so that if 'every', then also 'not every'. They do not, however, convert completely; for it is not the case that if 'not every', then already also 'every'. The same holds also for 'none' and 'some'.
"For affirmation and negation", that is, [there is] contradiction according to them between 'possibly of none' and 'of necessity of some'.
"For it is not, if it is not possible." Here he says clearly that to every contingent premise two premises of the necessary, taken together, are contradictory.

"For what of necessity does not hold of some A, it is not true to say that it is possible that it does not hold of every": since what is possible of none is possible also of every, to this, 'possibly of none', is opposed both 'of necessity not of every' and 'of necessity of some'; for if 'possibly of none', both 'of necessity not of every' and 'of necessity of some' are false.
