For what is possible of none is possible also of every; and through itself 'possibly of none' is opposed to 'of necessity of some', while through 'possibly of every' it is opposed to 'of necessity not of every'. So too 'possibly of every', through 'possibly of none', is opposed to 'of necessity of some', just as 'possibly of every' is opposed through itself to 'of necessity not of every'. He states only the surprising [cases]: that to 'possibly of none' 'of necessity not of every' is opposed, although both are negations, and to 'possibly of every' 'of necessity of some'; that is, to 'possibly of none', which he called 'possibly does not hold of every', 'of necessity not of every' is opposed, although both are negative, and to 'possibly of every' 'of necessity of some', although both are affirmative; for to the necessary [premises] unlike in quality it is obviously opposed.

"If then someone should claim." Let it be supposed that C holds of every D, but of some of necessity and of the others contingently, as motion [holds] of the heaven of necessity, but of the other [things] contingently; so 'C possibly of every D' is false, not because it does not hold of every, but because of some it does not hold contingently; and if 'possibly of every' is false, 'not possibly of every' is true; and when 'not possibly of every' is true, it is not only 'of necessity of some' that is true (for this is false), but also 'of necessity not of every'.
"He would be assuming something false"; for to 'possibly of every' not only 'of necessity of some' is opposed but also 'of necessity not of every'.

"For it holds of every, but because it holds of some of necessity, for this reason we say it is not possible of every." He states the reason why 'C possibly of every D' is false although it holds of every: because we say 'possibly of every' of what holds of some necessarily but not contingently.
"It is clear then that it is opposed to 'possible' in the sense whose definition we have given", that is, to [the possible] in the strict sense.

"So that no syllogism comes about", that is, no impossible conclusion comes about. If then someone should claim that only the obvious ones are opposed, 'of necessity of some' to 'possibly of none' and 'of necessity not of every' to 'possibly of every', and in general those of unlike form, he assumes falsely; for those of like form are opposed too, as has just been said.

"When this has been shown." Aristotle holds that all the combinations in the second figure from two contingent [premises] are non-syllogistic, not because it is peculiar to the second figure that the premises are of unlike form (for the contingent premises of the second figure, even if they are of like form, can become of unlike form; for he will give this as the cause only in the mixtures), nor because the contingent is either equally [possible] or for the most part or for the lesser part, and in no case universal, and from two particulars no syllogism comes about (for as far as this goes, there ought to be no syllogism from two contingent [premises] even in the first figure, nor any syllogistic mixture in the first figure having the major contingent); Aristotle, then, does not give these as the cause of no syllogism coming about in the second figure from two contingent [premises], but [says] that the syllogistic combinations in the second figure were shown either by conversion, as the first, second and third, or by reductio ad impossibile, as the fourth, and that neither can conversion be used now [nor reduction to the impossible] (for in conversion only the universal negative converted; and it has now been shown that the universal contingent negative does not convert into itself by simple conversion),

nor can reduction to the impossible be used. "For instance, A possibly of no B, A possibly of every C": he makes the argument again on the first mood, since the proof by reductio was common to all, even if it fitted only the fourth mood. If then something were concluded in the second figure, 'B possibly of no C' would be concluded; and if this is false, B of necessity of some C; and A possibly of no B; there comes about the first figure having the major contingent and for this reason concluding a contingent: A possibly not of every C; but also possibly of every; and nothing absurd [follows]. Nor does anything absurd follow in the fourth mood either. He shows them non-syllogistic not only in this way but also by their being refuted, like non-syllogistic [combinations], through terms; for it is easy to find terms concluding 'of necessity of none': white, man, horse; and if 'of necessity of none' is concluded, no contingent is concluded, neither affirmative nor negative, and for this reason there is no syllogism of the contingent. For Aristotle shows the contingent combinations non-syllogistic not in the customary way, by concluding 'of necessity of every' and 'of necessity of none', but is content with only one of the two, because of the reasoning stated. Alexander, however, sets out terms concluding 'of necessity of every' as well: white, animal, man. But perhaps, as long as white is possible of no animal, white is not possible of every man, as Alexander too observes much later. The Platonists, wishing syllogisms to come about in the second figure from two contingent [premises] as well, and as many as in the other modes, argue against these three arguments. Against the first they say that the universal contingent negative too converts into itself; for if A is separated from B, B too is separated from A. For Aristotle, in the case of the contingent, admits the contingent conversions but does not admit the simple ones; the Platonists the reverse. And the Platonists are more correct; for the syllogisms are about the contingent for the most part,

and in its case the contingent conversions do not hold, even if [they hold] in the case of the equally [possible], while the simple ones hold, even if in the case of the equally [possible] they do not hold. Against the second, that it is impossible for the same thing to be possible of the same thing both of every and not of every, as regards the contingent for the most part. Against the third, that the terms are not of the contingent for the most part but of the equally [possible].
SECOND FIGURE. MIXTURE OF CONTINGENT AND ASSERTORIC

"If one [premise is taken as] holding and the other as possible." Why does Aristotle, in this mixture, change the contingent negative into an affirmative, and not also the reverse? Because, says Alexander, the negatives here are in fact affirmatives and are taken by substitution into clearer affirmatives; but the affirmatives cannot be substituted into negatives in the strict sense while the mode is kept intact.

[Note] that in this mixture and the present figure those [moods] are syllogistic which, while the properties of the second figure are preserved, have an assertoric universal negative, whether they are from two universals or mixed, and those are non-syllogistic which do not have such a premise, an assertoric universal negative, whether the properties of the figure are preserved or not. And that for this reason the fourth mood is non-syllogistic; for not having a universal negative, neither will it have a universal negative of this kind. And that those having an assertoric universal negative conclude the half-contingent; for the assertoric universal negative becomes the major in the first figure; and it had been shown that in the mixture of contingent and assertoric, when the major is supposed an assertoric universal negative, the half-contingent is concluded. Those having the affirmative assertoric and the negative contingent, whether both universal or mixed, are non-syllogistic; for they can become of like form; and [also] for the general reason, since they do not have
an assertoric universal negative.
The proof is the same, [namely] that they can become of like form.

"If the affirmative is contingent." This [combination] is syllogistic, since it has an assertoric universal negative. And it is likewise syllogistic even if the assertoric universal negative is the minor; except that then we need two conversions, and the conclusion converts; for it is not a contingent universal negative but an assertoric universal negative; for what was concluded was the half-contingent.
"Just as in the earlier cases", that is, the half-contingent.
SECOND FIGURE. MIXTURE OF CONTINGENT AND NECESSARY.

When a mixture of contingent and necessary is made in the second figure, those [combinations] are syllogistic which have a necessary universal negative, whether both are universal or one universal and the other particular; except that in the mixed ones there is need of a further determination as well: for the necessary universal negative must be the major. And all conclude the half-contingent and [half-]necessary, and are imperfect, as being proved by reductio ad impossibile. And in short, what the assertoric universal negative did in the preceding mixture, the necessary universal negative now does. And the first mood needs one conversion, the second two. The one from two universal negatives having the major contingent [needs] three conversions, one contingent and two simple. And the fourth of the second figure is non-syllogistic; for if it has no universal negative at all, neither will it have a negative of this kind.
"Not only that it is possible for it not to hold,

but also that it does not hold." He calls the half-contingent and [half-]necessary "holding"; for what holds has something of the necessary, as having come about, and something of the contingent, as changing; and he calls this both "holding" and "contingent" for fear of the negation. And that the half-necessary and [half-]contingent is concluded, he shows thus: if "holds of none" is false, then "B necessarily [holds] of some C" is true, which again he calls "holds of some"; but A [holds] of B necessarily of none; therefore A [holds] of C necessarily not of every; but it is also possible of every; which is impossible; therefore B does not [hold] of C necessarily of some. And since nothing absurd follows also from "necessarily not of every", "of none" is concluded from necessity, which is said both of "necessarily of none" and of "possibly of none"; and because it is said sometimes of the necessary and sometimes of the contingent, it is half necessary and [half] contingent.

"At the same time it is clear" that what is concluded is not the contingent according to the qualification but the half-[contingent]; for if "holds of none" is false, "holds of some" is true; for what [holds] necessarily of some holds of some.

"And let it be possible for A to hold of no B, and let it hold of every C of necessity." This deduction is non-syllogistic, as not having a necessary universal negative; and it is non-syllogistic both of the contingent and of every conclusion: of the contingent, as concluding "of necessity of none"; for the necessary destroys every contingent; but neither is it syllogistic of the necessary, so that no one may suppose, because of the terms [giving] "of necessity of none", that it always concludes "of necessity of none". It is therefore non-syllogistic of the necessary, since those concluding a necessary [conclusion] had either both [premises] necessary or the necessary universal negative, so that we call the half-necessary too necessary; but now it is neither. And there are terms concluding "necessarily of every". And because of "of none" it concludes nothing affirmative, and because of "necessarily of every" nothing negative.
"For motion [belongs] to every waking of necessity";
for waking, as rousing, is a motion. But, they say, as long as motion is possible for every animal, nothing is waking such that it also moves. So the terms are not well chosen.
"Nor of the opposite affirmatives." The plural is right; for "necessarily of none" destroys every affirmative: necessary, assertoric, contingent.

"For let it be taken that A of necessity does not hold of B. And if the privative were placed with C, likewise." This is the one needing three conversions; for the premises convert and [so does] the conclusion.

"It is clear too that all are imperfect." A common conclusion about the two mixtures in the second figure, contingent and assertoric, contingent and necessary: that all are imperfect (for none was proved through "said of every and said of none", but all by reductio ad impossibile) and conclude the half-contingent.

"And they are perfected through the first figures." He spoke in the plural, since the first figure is [taken] in many ways; for the [mood] from contingent and assertoric in the second figure is perfected through the one from contingent and assertoric in the first figure, and the one from contingent and necessary in the second figure through the one from contingent and necessary in the first figure.
THIRD FIGURE FROM TWO CONTINGENTS.

"In the last figure." It is proper to the third figure, in [combinations] from two contingents, that one premise be universal; for from two particulars no syllogism comes about. There are now twelve syllogisms: for either both are universal, or one universal and the other particular, and this in two ways according to the major and minor premise, and each of the three in four ways according to quality. And each concludes the contingent in the strict sense.

"And when one is possible and the other holding." And yet then the contingent in the strict sense is not always concluded; for when the assertoric is a universal negative, the assertoric is concluded, just as also when the necessary is a universal negative, the half-contingent and [half-]necessary is concluded. Or [he says it] since the assertoric is contingent by not always being, as in the mixture of contingent
and assertoric he said the contingent is always concluded.

"Neither necessary nor holding, but the contingent in the strict sense." Next he calls the half-necessary and half-contingent "holding"; for what holds has from the one, the necessary, having come about, and from the other, the contingent, the not being able any longer to be.
"One must take in these too." When the necessary is a universal negative, one must take the contingent now too as the half-[contingent].

"When the premises are converted." And yet only one is converted, the minor. Or the same [premise], being "of none", first becomes "of every" by contingent conversion, then "of some" by simple conversion; so the converted premises are two, the "of none" and the "of every", even if both concern the [same] terms.

"The terms being related in the same way as in the case of holding." How is this not false, if in contingents the minor can be negative, but in the assertoric it cannot? Or not even in contingents does the minor produce a syllogism as negative, but as able to be substituted into an affirmative.
"And there is no syllogism." How is there no syllogism in [combinations] from two contingents? Either when the minor remains negative or when there is no universal premise.
THIRD FIGURE. MIXTURE OF CONTINGENT AND ASSERTORIC.

"If one is holding and the other possible." Eighteen syllogisms come about; for the six are doubled according to the order of the modes, and another six are added having the minor as contingent negative. For the same reasons there are as many syllogisms in the next mixture too. Proper to these two mixtures is that one be universal and the minor affirmative, if it is not contingent but assertoric or necessary.

"And not that it holds." And yet the assertoric is concluded when the assertoric is a universal negative. Or the assertoric is not always concluded, but the contingent always; for it is the common [element].

"There is a syllogism, the terms being related in the same way as in the earlier cases"; for as in the first and second figure, so now too in the mixtures of contingent and assertoric the contingent in the strict sense is concluded, unless the assertoric happens to be a universal negative.

"For when one of the premises." He ought to have said that the contingent in the strict sense is concluded, since it has been reduced to a mood of the first figure not having an assertoric universal negative; but instead of this he now says, and will say the same thing next, that the contingent is concluded, since it has been shown in the first figure that in the mixture of contingent and assertoric the conclusion follows the weaker [premise].

"If the affirmative is universal and the privative particular." The fifth mood, which is from "of every" and "not of every", having the universal assertoric and the particular contingent, he proves by reductio ad impossibile thus: A not of every C contingently; B of every C assertorically; I say that A is possible not of every B; for if not, A [holds] of every B of necessity, and B of every C assertorically; therefore A of every C of necessity; for the conclusion follows the major in the first figure in the mixture of assertoric and necessary; but it is also possible for A not [to hold] of every C; which is impossible. But why did he not prove this mood by conversion? Because it needed many conversions, namely four: for one would have had to make the major premise, the "not of every", into "of some", then convert the "of some" into itself by simple [conversion], then convert the conclusion "of some" into itself, then substitute it into "not of every", so that an affirmative is not concluded from an affirmative and a negative.
"The [syllogism] in universals and through the

same terms." But he did not give terms for the cases from two universal contingents, but for those from two particular contingents. Or else he now calls those from two particular contingents "universal" as having the contingent throughout.
THIRD FIGURE: MIXTURE OF CONTINGENT AND NECESSARY.

"If one of the premises is necessary and the other contingent." [Note] that when the necessary is a universal negative he says that both the contingent "of none" and the assertoric "of none" are concluded, but not "of none of necessity"; for the "not of any of necessity", which does away with the mode, is something other, and it is this that is concluded, as distinct from "of necessity of none".
"For so it turned out in the first figure." The contingent in the strict sense was concluded in the first figure when the necessary was not a universal negative.
"There will again be the first figure." Understand: "concluding the contingent in the strict sense"; for he adds the reason for this.
"Terms." Here he takes as middle the one middle in order of utterance, not the last one of the figure, [namely] horse. SLEEP SLEEPING MAN HORSE; SLEEP WAKING MAN HORSE

"It is clear, then, that in this figure too, when." When one is universal and the minor is affirmative, whether it is assertoric or necessary. "How": the contingent negative being changed into an affirmative, and either by conversion or by reductio ad impossibile.
"And when of being possible and when of holding." Those not having the necessary universal negative, he says, conclude the contingent in the strict sense.
SUMMARY OF THE MIXTURES.

There being three modes, assertoric, necessary, contingent, and also three figures, the mixtures are nine in all. And in the mixture of assertoric and necessary, in the first figure he holds that the conclusion follows the major; in the second, the one that is converted in the reduction to the first figure; in the third, the one that is not converted, that is, when the proof comes about by conversion; but if only by reductio ad impossibile, as in the fourth [mood] of the second and the fifth of the third, the weaker. In the remaining six mixtures [he holds] that the contingent in the strict sense is concluded, unless the [premise] combined with the contingent premise happens to be a universal negative, whether assertoric or necessary; for then in [the mixture of] contingent and assertoric the assertoric is concluded, and in [that of] contingent and necessary the half-contingent and [half-]necessary. But his associates and the Platonists hold that in the nine mixtures the conclusion always follows the weaker.
ON THE MIXTURES.

"That the [syllogisms] in these figures, then." Having taught all the categorical syllogisms, simple and mixed, Aristotle now reduces all syllogisms, categorical, hypothetical, direct, by reductio ad impossibile, simple, compound, to the three figures. And first the simple categorical ones, which are in any case direct, in this way: if one has to prove the premise AB, either we shall take nothing or we shall take something for establishing it; if the former, we shall be begging the original question; if the latter, either one thing or many; if one, no syllogism comes about, for it comes about when certain things are laid down, not when one thing is laid down; if many, either two or more; and if two, they are attached to both terms A and B; for a syllogism simply is from premises simply, a syllogism of this from [the] premises of this, a syllogism in relation to that from premises in relation to that, and a syllogism of this in relation to that from premises of this in relation to that. So

the two premises will have a common term; and this is either predicated in both or is subject in both or mixed; and the three figures come about. Likewise the compound categorical syllogism too is reduced to the three figures; for its principal premises are two, and the others make prosyllogisms, as he shows next. And the syllogisms by reductio ad impossibile, being compound hypotheticals, also fall under the three figures; and so do the simple hypotheticals; those by reductio because they need a categorical syllogism to prove the impossibility, as for example the geometrical theorem that shows through a categorical syllogism how, if the diagonal is commensurable with the side, the same number is both even and odd; and the simple hypotheticals, that is, the direct ones, because they need a categorical syllogism to prove the additional premise; for, Aristotle says, in hypothetical syllogisms the conditional must be agreed in any case, and the additional premise must be in doubt. And both [requirements] are right: for if the conditional were in doubt, it would also be in doubt whether they are hypothetical, and the one establishing the conditional would at the same time establish that they are hypothetical; and if the additional premise too were agreed, there would be no need of a hypothetical syllogism. And in another way, generally, every hypothetical, direct and by reductio, needs a categorical syllogism; for if we always establish hypotheses through a hypothesis, we shall never come to a stop. If then every hypothetical syllogism needs a categorical, and every categorical comes about through the three figures, then every hypothetical, and every syllogism, needs the three figures. And for this reason every proof is reduced to the first figure, and [the proofs] of the first figure to the universal syllogisms.

"That, then." Since it has been shown that the syllogisms in the three figures are reduced to the first figure and to the two universal syllogisms of the first, we shall now show that every [categorical] syllogism too

is so, if we first show that every categorical syllogism is reduced to the three figures; and not only is every categorical syllogism so, but also every hypothetical, of which the one by reductio is a part; for every [syllogism] by reductio is hypothetical, but not every hypothetical is by reductio, just as every categorical is direct, but not every direct one is categorical; for this is direct but not categorical: a number is either even or odd; but it is not even; therefore it is odd.
"And C of nothing." So that it is the first figure: A of C, C of D.
"Nor anything else of that." So that it is the third figure: A and D of C. The second he passed over as being introduced through the extremes.
"Nor anything else of A." Again the first figure: D of A, A of C.
"If, then, A is taken of something else or something else of A." [Note] that the premises must not be connected only to the major term.
"Or something else of C." So that it is the third figure: A 〈and D〉 of C. And again the premises are connected only to the major.
"Nor when." [Note] that the premises must depend on both extremes of the conclusion.
"For the same argument." [Note] that every compound categorical is reduced to one of the three figures; for its principal premises are two, and the others make a prosyllogism.

〈"That the probative ones, then."〉 [Note] that he calls the direct ones "probative" and those by reductio "circuitous", since the direct ones are concise, as proving the proposition straight off (for the straight line is the shortest of all lines having the same endpoints, whence "straightway" is also said from "straight"), while those by reductio travel a long road doing away with the opposites in order to bring in the propositions; whence in ordinary usage too we speak of a "circuit" for things needing a long supposition.

"They deduce what is false in reaching their conclusion." [Note] that Aristotle calls the categorical a syllogism even simply, but the hypothetical a syllogism only with the qualifier, never a syllogism simply,

just as [he does] not [call] a dead man simply a man. So the impossibility, he says, in the hypothetical syllogism is proved by a categorical syllogism, for example that the same number is at once even and odd if the diagonal is commensurable with the side. But the proposition is proved by the hypothetical syllogism: since the diagonal is either commensurable or incommensurable with the side, and it is not commensurable because of some categorical lemma, it is therefore incommensurable. Hence the one by reductio is called hypothetical even though it also uses a categorical syllogism, since the categorical is a lemma, while the hypothetical proves the proposition.
[Note] that he calls "contradiction" the part opposed to what is proposed for proof.

"Likewise." [Note] that not only those hypotheticals that are by reductio are reduced to the three figures, but generally all hypotheticals; for the direct hypotheticals too [are]; for they prove the doubtful points in hypotheticals through a categorical syllogism, so as not to proceed to infinity always proving the previously assumed hypotheses through a hypothesis.

[Note] that what the Stoics call the "additional premise" Aristotle here calls "substitution", because it is substituted from a doubtful [statement] into an agreed one; for it is no longer stated with "if" but with "but". But by "prosleptic form" Aristotle means the premise equivalent to a syllogism, which has two terms in actuality and one potentially: of whatever man [is predicated], of that [is predicated] animal.

[Note] that it is a doctrine of Aristotle that in hypotheticals the conditional is agreed and that the additional premise is in every case established, and we have shown both of these to be true in the lecture.

[Note] that not only are the hypotheticals mixed from a categorical and a hypothetical syllogism reduced to the three figures by means of the categorical, but so too are the wholly hypothetical ones: if man, then animal; if animal, then animate; therefore if man, animate. And the syllogisms by prosleptic form too

are reduced to the three figures: of whatever A [is predicated], B too [is predicated]; for it is the third figure. And the wholly hypothetical and the prosleptic ones do not come under the three figures through the medium of something else, as all the mixed hypotheticals do, but through their own combination. So every construction is reduced to the three figures; and this was what was proposed.
ON HYPOTHETICAL SYLLOGISMS, FROM THE SINGLE BOOK OF AMMONIUS.

Since Aristotle worked out the categorical syllogisms in detail without omission—all the simple ones, all the mixed ones, all the figures, all the moods—but does not appear to have taken much care over the technical treatment of the hypotheticals (for he says only this about them: that those by reductio are a part of those from a hypothesis, and that both those by reductio and the direct hypotheticals are reduced to the three figures by needing a categorical syllogism that establishes either the falsehood or the additional premise), and since he bids us at the end of the second section of this book to divide up the hypotheticals, saying "one must examine and divide in how many ways [syllogisms] from a hypothesis [occur]", come, let us do what has been ordered, and let us investigate these eight [questions] about the hypotheticals. 1. Why did Aristotle not expand his account of the hypotheticals too? Either because the Stoics had treated them with precision; or because these are not syllogisms simply, but the whole thing is syllogisms from a hypothesis; or because he was content with the categoricals, since the hypotheticals too [proceed] through these. 2. What are the names the Stoics use? Well, they call things "objects" (*tynchanonta*), for the goal is to attain (*tychein*) them; thoughts "expressibles" (*ekphorika*), for we express (*ekpherein*) these through spoken sounds; spoken sounds "sayables" (*lekta*); the conditional or the disjunctive "tropic" (*tropikon*), because it makes a turn (*tropos*) from one proposition to another. The antecedent they call antecedent, as we do; the consequent "terminating" (*lēgon*); the additional premise additional premise, as we do. But Aristotle

calls it "substitution", because it is substituted from doubt into actuality; for it is no longer stated with a doubting conjunction. And Aristotle [speaks] better; for no other [premise] beyond what was proposed is added, as [happens] in what he himself shortly after calls a premise by prosleptic form, "of whatever man [is predicated], of that animal too"; for there is added "and man [is predicated] of Socrates". What we call a conclusion, they call an *epiphora* [inference]. And the hypothetical syllogisms they call "indemonstrables" and "themata". 3. The likeness and unlikeness of categorical and hypothetical syllogisms. What the two premises are in categoricals, that in hypotheticals is the conditional or disjunctive and the additional premise; what the minor is there, that here is the antecedent; and what the major is, that is the consequent and the additional premise; and what the middle term is in categoricals, that here is the conjunction "if", say, or "or", and in short the relation; for sometimes a participle too connects, as in "the sun being above the earth, it is day". They differ in that in categoricals both premises were agreed, and a conclusion is established as a third thing beyond them, whereas here only one is clear, and the other is established through it. 4. How many are the kinds of hypothetical syllogisms? They are those written below. First, the one from consequence, which by positing the antecedent posits the consequent: if man, then animal; but the first; therefore the second. Second, the one from consequence, which by denying the consequent denies the antecedent: if man, then animal; but not animal; therefore not man. If not animal, then not man; but man; therefore animal. This is also called conversion with opposition. Third, the one from separation and negative conjunction, which denies by positing: not both man and horse [are] the same thing; but man; therefore not horse. Fourth, the one from separation, which denies by positing: either it is day or night; but it is day; therefore not night.

Fifth, the one from separation, which posits by denying: either it is day or night; but it is not day; therefore it is night. There are only five for this reason: two kinds of matter produce one syllogism—for whether the propositions are not opposed, or are mediately opposed, the third syllogism results—while one kind of matter, immediate opposites, produces two syllogisms, the fourth and the fifth. [Diagram:] conjoined / disjoined; establishes / refutes; opposed / not opposed; A B; immediate / mediate; C; from positing / from denying; C D E. 5. The reason for the order of the hypothetical syllogisms. Since association is better than difference, those by continuity precede those by separation. And since being is better than not being, among those by continuity the constructive precede the destructive. And since the universal is better than the particular, among those by separation the one ranging over the three kinds of matter is prior to the one over only two, and this to the one over only one; for one can say "not both man and horse [are] the same thing", which are not opposed, and "not white and black the same thing", which are mediately opposed, and "not even and odd the same [number]", which are immediately opposed. Then how in the division did we take the third over two kinds of matter? Because if they are immediately opposed, one may also not use the third mood, but either the fourth or the fifth; but if [it is] the other two sections, it is not possible to establish [it] otherwise than through the third. So the division is into what is necessary, not into what is possible and redundant. 6. What is reduction to the impossible? It is composed of three syllogisms, two hypothetical and one categorical, and the hypotheticals are the fifth and the second; the fifth proves the proposition, the second the additional premise of the fifth, and the categorical the conditional of the second;

hence it is also called hypothetical although it has a categorical syllogism too as a part, since the proposition is proved through the fifth mood of the hypotheticals, while the categorical is a lemma. For example: the diagonal of the square is either commensurable or incommensurable with the side; but it is not commensurable, as I shall show; therefore through the fifth of the hypotheticals it is incommensurable, which was proposed to be shown. And the diagonal is not commensurable with the side for these reasons: if the diagonal is commensurable with the side, the same number is both even and odd, as I shall show; but the second is not the case; therefore through the second of the hypotheticals neither is the first. And that, if the diagonal is commensurable with the side, the same [number] turns out even and odd, the geometrical theorem proves through a categorical syllogism. So those by reductio are a part of those from a hypothesis, if every [syllogism] by reductio is hypothetical, but not every hypothetical is by reductio; for the five moods certainly are not, being direct. The one by reductio is also called circuitous, as not proving the proposition straightforwardly; for the syllogism of the proposition [itself] is called direct, since the straight line too is the shortest of those having the same endpoints.
ON SYLLOGISMS BY PROSLEPTIC FORM.

These, then, have from the categoricals the feature of occurring in all the figures: in the first, "to whatever C [belongs] in every case, to that A [belongs] in every case"; in the second, "what [is said] of every B, that [is said] also of every C"; in the third, "of whatever A [is said] in every case, of that B too"; but here an affirmative is concluded even in the second, and a universal in the third, and [a conclusion follows] from two negatives in all [figures], and non-belonging is concluded from belonging. From the hypotheticals they have the conjunction of the premises and the establishing of one through the other; but they are neither wholly hypothetical, nor are they reduced under the five moods.
Syllogisms by prosleptic form are categorical in that they occur in the three figures. They are not categorical in that they do not preserve the properties

of the figures. They are hypothetical because the two premises are conjoined and one is established through the other. They are not hypothetical, for they are neither wholly [hypothetical] nor not wholly [so]; the second, because they do not come under the five moods.

"Further, in every [syllogism] there must be." He hands down theorems common to the three figures. First: there is no syllogism without a universal premise; for one from two particulars does not reason syllogistically, and either does not [prove] the proposition, or begs the original question. For if one must show that musical pleasure is good, [and] one speaks thus, "musical pleasure is pleasure; pleasure is good; therefore musical pleasure is good", one does not reason syllogistically; for it has been shown that from two particulars nothing follows necessarily. And then, when one says "pleasure is good", if one says it with an eye to geometrical pleasure, the proposition is not concluded; but if with an eye to musical pleasure, one will be begging the original question. But it is better to make not three divisions but two: [such a person] in any case does not reason syllogistically; and where [he concludes] nothing, [he concludes] not the proposition either; or [he concludes] the proposition, but along with that begs the original question. So let the geometers not say, "since A is equal to B, and B is equal to C, therefore A too is equal to C"; for they conclude truths not because of the combination but because of the matter; which is why the Stoics too say that they conclude unmethodically.

But let them make the two particulars into one particular and add the universal; for example: A and B are equal to the same thing; all things equal to the same thing are also equal to each other; therefore A and B are equal to each other. Or, as the text has it, let them not say, "since these [angles] of the semicircles are equal, of which these of the segment are equal, therefore the remaining ones, these at the base of the isosceles triangle, are equal", but rather thus: "these [angles] of the isosceles are what remain when equals are taken away from equals; all things remaining after the taking away of equals from equals are equal; therefore these [angles] of the isosceles triangle are equal." And "this is equal to that" is particular not because of its demonstrative [form] (for geometers everywhere frame their argument about universals), but because the indefinite is equivalent to the particular.

The second [theorem] common to the three figures: the conclusion does not in every case resemble one of the premises, neither in quantity nor in quality: in quantity, since in the third figure a particular is concluded from two universals; in quality, since, even if in respect of affirmative and negative, and assertoric, necessary and contingent, it resembles either both premises or at any rate one, it certainly does not do so in respect of falsehood and truth, which are themselves also qualities and modes; for a truth is concluded even from two falsehoods.

[Note] that, having said that no syllogism arises from two negations or particulars, he works out only the second. "For let it be laid down", that is, let it be proposed for inquiry, whether musical pleasure is good.

AC and BD he calls the angles of the semicircles, CD those of the segment, EF those of the triangle; for he also divides the letters of the angles of the semicircles into the letters of the angles of the segment and of the triangle; and the sides of the triangle he calls AB. There are three syllogisms: the angles AC, BD are angles of equal semicircles; all the angles of equal semicircles

are equal; therefore the angles AC, BD are equal. Again, CD are angles of the same segment; all angles of the same segment are equal by superposition; therefore the angles CD are equal. Again, the angles EF of the triangle are what remain after the taking away of equals from equals; all things remaining by the taking away of equals from equals are equal; therefore the angles EF of the triangle too are equal; which [...] some say that [one should] speak thus: "since AC, BD are equal, of which CD are equal, therefore the remaining angles EF of the isosceles triangle are equal", erring in two ways: for both [premises] are particular, since indefinite; and because they have left out the major [premise], which has authority in syllogisms and holds the status of an axiom, and have divided the minor into two. And hence they beg the original question; for what they have not shown, they think they have shown.

"But also in being necessary or assertoric or contingent." How then, in the second and third figures, in the mixture of contingent and necessary, when the necessary [premise] is universal negative, is the half-contingent and [half-]necessary concluded? Or does it resemble [them] even then? For "to none by necessity" is concluded, which applies both to "to none of necessity" and to "possibly to none"; so it resembles both.

"And to examine the other predications too." So he himself also knows that the conclusion does not always follow one of the premises in quality, if indeed a truth is concluded from falsehoods. He called the modes predications since, if being subject seems to belong to matter, being predicated would belong to form, which is the same as saying to quality or mode.
[Note] that he calls the imperfect [syllogism] possible, as being potentially perfect.

"And it is clear too that every demonstration." Having shown that every simple categorical syllogism comes about through one of the three figures, and that every hypothetical too, by reductio and direct, which is the same as saying compound and simple, is reduced under the three figures through the medium of a simple

categorical [syllogism] which establishes either the conditional, as in those by reductio, or the additional premise, as in the direct ones, he now shows what remains, that every compound categorical syllogism is reduced under the three figures through the medium of the [syllogism] that proves proximately, which in every case is from three terms. And first he argues for the opposite, that the categorical syllogism which proves proximately can be from more terms than three; for it can be from more than three both in relation and in substrate. In relation, since it is possible to show that not every man is white through the same middle, the Ethiopian, in the three figures, as is set out below; for this reason the problem taken is particular negative, as the only one of the problems proved in the three figures. So the three terms, [the same] in substrate, have become nine in relation. And he resolves it by saying that the syllogisms are many (namely three); but what was proposed to be shown was not that many syllogisms are from three terms, but that one syllogism is in every case from three terms. Second argument in favour: in substrate too it is possible for the terms of the syllogism to be more than three, if indeed it is possible to prove the same problem now through one middle, now through another, as Plato [proves] the immortality of the soul in the Phaedo through the middle "bringing life to the body"; for nothing admits the contrary of what it brings [where the self-moved is immortal]; and in the tenth [book] of the Republic, saying: the soul is not destroyed by its own vice; for on the contrary the wicked seem both more full of life and alone to live, because of their greed and luxury; what is not destroyed by its own vice is indestructible, since everything that is destroyed is destroyed by its own vice, as iron and bronze by rust, grain by

blight. But here again the syllogisms are many, all the more as the premises of the syllogisms stand further apart from one another; and as many as the middles are, so many are the syllogisms. And the same problem [is proved] through more terms than three, but not the one syllogism under discussion. Third argument in favour: it is possible for a categorical syllogism to proceed through more terms than three, as Plato in the Phaedrus proved the soul immortal through the middle of the self-moved and the ever-moving. But again there are two syllogisms: that the soul is ever-moving, through the middle of the self-moved, and that it is immortal, through the middle of the ever-moving.

That every syllogism is from two proximate premises he shows thus: if possible, let E be concluded from four proximate premises, A B C D. Then the premises A B either conclude something or do not conclude [anything]; but if they do not conclude anything, they have been taken in vain; and if they conclude something, they conclude either E, or one of the remaining premises C D, or something else besides these; but if E, we have what is sought, that the syllogism is from two premises; if one of C D, the syllogism is no longer proximate or simple but compound, from a prosyllogism; and if A B conclude something other than E and C D, now not only are the syllogisms many, as in the second supposition too, but also unconnected with one another. And what has been said of A B will fit C D too; for again C D either conclude something or do not; and if they do not, they have been taken in vain; and if they do, if E, the premises A B are redundant, and every syllogism is from two proximate premises; if one of A B, the syllogisms will be many, one a prosyllogism, the other [the syllogism] of the proposition; and if something other than A B, plainly the syllogisms are many; for the syllogisms are unconnected with one another, and the continuity of the premises, giving the appearance of one, does not cancel this.
"And that every demonstration." He has called every establishing argument
a demonstration.
"If not through different and different [terms]." Either in relation, as in the first argument in favour, or in substrate, as in the second.

"For example E through A B and through C D." This is an example of the second argument in favour, the one that concludes the same thing, E say, through terms that differ in substrate, for example A B and C D; for A B differ from C D in substrate.

"Or through A B and B C and A C." This is an example of the first argument in favour, where the same thing, for example E, is concluded through [terms] differing in relation only; that is why A B and B C and A C have one term in common and one different; for the second [figure] arises from the first when the major is converted, and the third when the minor is. So A B is the first figure, and A is the major premise and B the minor; and in the second figure, B C, the minor of A B, namely B, remained; while in the third figure, A C, the major of A B, namely A, remained.
"But if these are so, the syllogisms are not one but many." The resolution of the two arguments in favour: the syllogism did not remain one, even if the problem did.

"Or again when each." The third argument in favour, which is also the more persuasive, and so he thinks it worthy of a special resolution: the one that takes the premises of a single syllogism as mediated. And he resolves this by saying that the syllogisms are three, since the conclusions too are three, the two premises and the conclusion; for the former are conclusions of the prosyllogisms, the latter of the syllogism.

"Or one by induction and the other by syllogism." For example, if the problem were that medicine is useful to life, and we said: medicine is an art, every art is useful to life, so medicine too [is useful]; and we shall establish the minor through a syllogism: medicine is a method that makes a way, every method that makes a way is an art, so medicine too is an art; and the major, that every art is useful to life, by induction: for so are farming and weaving. Or as Plato [does] in the Republic: for when Thrasymachus has called justice bad counsel, he himself establishes
that the just man is wise, speaking thus:
the just man does 〈not〉 wish to have more than one like him; the wise man does not wish to have more than one like him, but wishes to have more than one unlike him.
And of these premises he establishes the minor taking as middle "what assigns according to worth", and the second by induction from the doctor, the seer, the geometer.

"If then not more but one." If anyone, he says, should call the syllogism through five terms, or through however many, one, looking to the continuity of the premises, we shall not begrudge him the name, except that it is one remotely, not one proximately; for this is what "in this way it is possible" and "but as C through A B, impossible" indicate. And that it is not one proximately, he adds the demonstration. Of the four premises A B C D concluding E, A B, he says, are either combined syllogistically, so that one is the major and the other the minor, in place of which he himself said "whole and part", or non-syllogistically. And if the first, they conclude either E, or one of C D, or something else besides these. And he refutes only the first, saying: how too is E, which is supposed [to follow] from A B C D, concluded from A B alone? And before refuting the remaining suppositions about A B he goes over to C D as well; for these too either conclude something or not. And if they conclude, [they conclude] either E, or one of A B, or something else besides these. And if one of A B, the syllogisms will be more, since the conclusions are too, and C D is a prosyllogism of A B C D. And if E, if the syllogisms are A B C D and C D, though it is possible [to call them] one, by concluding the same thing, still they are not in truth one; and he points to the syllogisms about the Ethiopian in the three figures through the same terms. And if C D [conclude] not one of A B either but something else besides these, not only will the syllogisms be many, A B C D and C D, but also unconnected with one another. And if C D conclude nothing, they have been taken in the syllogism in vain, unless indeed they have been brought in for the sake of

induction or concealment or for some other such reason. Then he goes back again to the remaining suppositions about A B. And [brought in] for induction, as we showed every art useful to life through farming and weaving. And for the sake of concealment, because one should not ask the two premises in succession, since the person questioned, noticing, becomes more inclined to object; rather one ought to insert in between something akin to the premise asked, then bring on the other. For example, if the problem were that pleasure is good, and we took that pleasure is desirable, let us not say at once "What then? Is everything desirable good?", but let us draw out an account of the desirable: that the beautiful (kalon) calls (kalei) to itself, and the good (agathon) is that towards which all things run eagerly (agan thei). And if someone wishing to show health is good says "health is good for the good man", let him not at once add "and what is good for such a man is truly good", but let him say in between how health comes about, namely when the doctor adjudicates between the elements and the humours. Sometimes too [it is inserted] for management of the argument: for example, the virtues are choiceworthy for their own sake, even if they bring no profit. Sometimes too, because of the dryness of dialectical argument, it is put in for the sake of adorning the argument. And sometimes also for clarity, as in comparisons: that as one perception is of contraries, so too is knowledge. Sometimes too, because the argument looks to display, we swell it with insertions.

"But if from A B not E but something else results as conclusion, and from C D either one of these or something else besides these." He goes back again to A B and refutes the remaining suppositions; for he refuted only one, the one concluding E. For if, he says, A B conclude not E but something else, and this other thing happens to be, from C D, either one of these or [something] elsewhere and besides these, then if one of C D, it is a prosyllogism of the syllogism, and for this reason the syllogism is not one but many; and if something other than C D, A B too have been taken in vain, if they were taken for the sake of E,
and they neither conclude this nor anything else that concludes it.

"But if nothing results from C D." The error is a scribal one from the beginning; for he should have said "from A B"; for it has already been said about C D what follows if they conclude nothing, but about A B it has not been said. And as far as the transmitted reading goes, Aristotle is both prattling and omitting, saying one thing twice and the other not even once.
"Unless it is taken in addition", that is, unless again it is taken for the sake of concealment or induction or adornment of the argument.

"So a syllogism which does not have two premises", that is, only three terms concluding the principal conclusion (for there are also non-principal conclusions, like those of prosyllogisms), this argument either has not been syllogized, as if someone were to take many particular premises having nothing in common, or has asked superfluous things besides the necessary ones, as if someone wishing to show that man is an animal were to say "man is capable of laughing, what is capable of laughing is an animal, animal is animate, so man is an animal"; for the premise saying that animal is animate is superfluous.

"So according to the principal premises." Having shown that every simple categorical syllogism is from three [terms], he hands down two consequences of this: that of the proximate categorical syllogism the premises are even, and the terms odd; for he calls the first even and the first odd by the proper name "even" simply and "odd" simply. And the conclusion is half of the premises and a third of the terms; and the intervals are one fewer than the terms. But when the syllogism is compound, only one of the things said is preserved, that the intervals are one fewer than the terms; for this is true whether the added [term] is packed in or inserted from outside; but it is no longer in every case that the premises are even and the terms odd, but it is possible [for it to be] the other way round too. Never, however, are both even, both the premises and the terms, but [they are] mixed, because at the outset they differed from one another by even and odd, and a unit is added to each, and the kind, even or odd, is changed

when a unit is added; and a unit is added to each, since when a term is added, whether by packing in or from outside, one premise is added. But the conclusions are no longer half of the premises and a third of the terms; rather they sometimes exceed in number both the premises and the terms; and by premises I mean those that are only premises. For when there are five terms, there come to be four premises, but six conclusions; for in general, with each addition of a term, whether it is added from outside or inserted, conclusions are added one fewer than the terms already there. The reason is that the added [term] does not make a conclusion only with the next one in order.
ON ESTABLISHING AND REFUTING PROBLEMS.

"And since we have [said] what the syllogisms are about", up to the end of the first section, the one on the generation of syllogisms. Through these words Aristotle shows that universals are readier than particulars for refutation than for establishing, and particulars, on the contrary, readier for establishing than for refutation. For he assumes beforehand that "to every" is shown in one way only, "to none" in three ways, in the first [figure] in one way, in the second in two ways; "to some" in four ways, in the first in one way, in the third in three ways; "not to every" in six ways, in the first in one way, in the second in two ways, in the third in three ways. With these assumed, each of the four problems is established and refuted in so many ways:
IS ESTABLISHED: "to every" in one way; "to none" in three ways; "to some" in four ways; "not to every" in six ways
IS REFUTED: in six ways, through "not to every"; in four ways, through "to some"; in three ways, through "to none"; in one way, through "to every".
So since universals are established in one way or three ways, and particulars in four ways or six ways, particulars are easier to argue for

than universals with a view to establishing. And since universals are refuted in six ways or four ways, and particulars in three ways or one way, universals are therefore easier to argue against than particulars with a view to refutation.

Second argument. If the universal is destroyed both through the contrary and through the contradictory, but the particular through the contradictory alone, then the universal is more readily destroyed than the particular. And that the universal is also harder to establish than the particular, the text shows in two ways: for of the particulars, "not to every" [is shown] in more figures than the universals, and "to some" through more moods than the universals. But since this belongs to the first argument, he adds a newer establishing argument of this kind: particulars are more readily established than universals, since universals are shown through themselves alone, but particulars both through themselves and through universals; for if "to every", also "to some", and if "to none", also "not to every".
"What the syllogisms are about", that is, the problems; for he adds also which kind is difficult and which easier to argue, whether for establishing or for refutation.

"So it is evident that the universal affirmative." For it is established in one way only, but refuted in six ways. And similarly in the case of the rest. The second argument divides the four into two, into universals and particulars, through [the words] "and in general it is easier for one refuting [to refute] universals than particulars."
"And in the case of the privatives." For "to none" is destroyed both through "to every" and through "to some", which [i.e. "to none" or "to some"] are shown in two figures.

"But easier for one establishing." The remaining part of the second argument, which is also shown in two ways: first from particulars being shown in more ways than universals, either by figures or by moods.

"And in general one should not." Not as, he says, universals are destroyed through particulars and particulars through universals, so too are particulars established through universals and universals through particulars; but

particulars are inferred through universals, but no longer universals through particulars, but through themselves alone; for if "to every", also "to some"; but not if "to some", also "to every". And since particulars are established in two ways, both through themselves and through the universals that contain them, but universals in one way only (for through themselves alone), particulars are readier than universals for establishing; but it has been shown that universals are easier to argue against than particulars for refutation; so, in sum, universals, as compared with particulars (for this must be understood in addition), are easier to refute than to establish.

"How then every syllogism comes about, both the direct one and the one by reductio ad impossibile." "Comes about" [is said] properly, since the section is about the generation of syllogisms. Or: how the categorical and the hypothetical come about; for both are reduced to the three figures, the categorical in their entirety, the hypothetical through the establishing arguments either of the impossible or of the additional premise. "And through how many terms": that [it is] three, the proximate ones.

"And how [the premises] are disposed": either according to the simple and compound [forms] of the categorical syllogism, or according to the categorical and hypothetical [forms] of the syllogism in general.

And because of the numbers, particulars are easier than universals to argue for establishing, but harder to argue for refutation; and because, as in the second argument, particulars are established in two ways, universals in one way only, while particulars are refuted in one way only, universals in two ways.
